Instructional Design · 2026
Compliance Training · Self-Paced · 10 Modules

Teaching GRC staff to read and apply a 75-page compliance standard.

A self-paced course that prepares Governance, Risk, and Compliance (GRC) professionals to read, interpret, and apply the AICPA Trust Services Criteria. The content is drawn from the primary source and cited to it by paragraph, and the course uses a custom design system and fourteen engagement types.

The design language at a glance

A warm, approachable design system built for newcomers to dense regulatory material. Each module is presented one lesson at a time, and color distinguishes the kinds of learning content: orientation, vocabulary, worked examples, activities, and checkpoints.

Methodology

Grounded in established frameworks

Each design decision corresponds to a recognized instructional design framework. The learning design document describes each alignment in detail.

B

Bloom's Taxonomy

Anderson & Krathwohl, 2001

Cognitive progression from Remember (M1–M3) through Apply (M4–M8) to Evaluate / Create (M10). Module objectives written as observable behaviors at the targeted level.

M

Mayer's Multimedia Principles

Mayer, 2009

Coherence, signaling, segmenting, spatial contiguity, personalization, and feedback. These principles account for the visual restraint, color-coded callouts, inline definitions, and full-paragraph knowledge check explanations.

K

Kirkpatrick's Four Levels

Kirkpatrick & Kirkpatrick, 2016

Reaction, Learning, Behavior, and Results. Assessment built into the course addresses Levels 1 and 2; the deployment plan documents Levels 3 and 4 through seven observable behaviors and five organization-level metrics.

Key design decisions

Decisions that shaped the course

The rationale for each choice and its relation to the needs of the audience.

01

Outcome-based framing

TSP 100, para. .03, frames the TSC as outcome-based. The course establishes this principle in M1, reinforces it in M8, where learners build controls, and presents it in M10 as one of five mental models. The most common misconception among GRC staff, that SOC 2 is a checklist, is addressed on the first screen.

02

Fidelity to the source text

Compliance training in this domain often resembles marketing copy. The course was written from the source text outward, with careful paraphrase and paragraph citations throughout. This approach establishes credibility with a skeptical professional audience.

03

Engagement variety as a cognitive tool

The course uses fourteen interaction types, each matched to a specific cognitive task. Sorting reinforces categorical recognition, hotspots train pattern-matching, and flashcards support durable recall.

04

Optional capstone, mandatory mental models

The original outline made course completion contingent on a 15-question capstone; the final design reverses this. Working professionals may not have time for a required assessment on a first pass. The mental models and role-based playbooks form the core of Module 10, and the capstone is optional, with a "skip to wrap" link.

05

Reference-grade Module 9

Module 9 has no knowledge check because it is designed as a permanent working tool for use after the course ends. It contains 93 searchable glossary terms with PDF and Practice source badges, three quick-lookup tables, six source-document cards, and an 18-card flashcard set.

06

Iterative review and revision

Three rounds of structured review identified visual breakage at scale (badges, sort items), CSS class collisions in the consolidated deployment, and gaps in PDF coverage. Each round was documented, and each fix was verified.

Needs Analysis

Performance gap · learners · tasks · success measures

Trust Services Criteria for GRC Staff

Needs analysis for a self-paced course on TSP Section 100

Subject matter: AICPA Trust Services Criteria (TSP Section 100, 2017 criteria with revised points of focus, 2022)
Target performers: Governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) staff at SaaS service organizations
Proposed solution: Self-paced web course, 10 modules, with a complementary job aid
Status: Portfolio project; the analysis is documentary and assumption-based, as described in Section 1

1. Purpose, scope and method

This analysis determines whether training is an appropriate response to the difficulties GRC staff encounter with the Trust Services Criteria, identifies the part of the performance gap that training can close, and defines the learners, tasks, content and success measures on which the course design rests. Its scope is the use of TSP 100 by staff at service organizations that prepare for or maintain SOC 2 examinations. The work of the service auditor, and other engagements that use the criteria, fall outside the scope.

The project was developed as a portfolio piece without a client organization. No stakeholder interviews, surveys or organizational records were available, and none are reported. The analysis draws on four sources:

  1. The source standard. A close reading of TSP 100, including paragraphs .01–.29, the criteria and points of focus table, the privacy markers and the glossary.
  2. The GRC role. The tasks GRC staff perform with the criteria across the SOC 2 cycle, derived from the standard and the practices it presupposes.
  3. Existing materials. The original course outline and a content gap analysis that compared an earlier draft of Modules 1–5 with the source document.
  4. Explicit assumptions. Conditions that only an organization could confirm are stated as assumptions; Section 11 lists each with its validation method.

Statements about learner difficulty therefore describe typical, documented difficulty areas reasoned from the standard and the content review. They are not measured findings.

2. Problem statement

GRC staff are expected to read the criteria accurately, apply them to their organization's system, and produce scoping decisions, control narratives, evidence and a system description that a service auditor can test. The source document is long and legalistic, and several of its conventions are explained only briefly or in footnotes. The table states the gap as typical current performance against desired performance.

Performance area Typical current performance Desired performance Basis in the standard
Points of focus Staff treat the points of focus as a mandatory checklist and attempt to evidence each one Staff treat the criteria as the required outcomes and use points of focus as guidance, customizing or adding to them where circumstances warrant TSP 100, paras. .04–.07
Category scoping Categories are selected by habit or customer request, without reference to service commitments and system requirements Staff select categories from documented commitments and requirements and can explain the criteria each category adds TSP 100, paras. .10–.15, .19
Criterion applicability Criteria are excluded without justification, or every criterion is retained when one is clearly irrelevant to the services provided Staff recognize the limited circumstances in which a criterion does not apply and document the reason TSP 100, para. .11
Interpretation The phrase "to meet the entity's objectives" is read generically Staff read the phrase as the service organization's commitments and system requirements in a SOC 2 engagement TSP 100, paras. .18–.24
Control mapping Controls are mapped loosely, often one control to one criterion by keyword Staff map each control to every criterion whose outcome it supports and can state how it does so TSP 100, para. .03; criteria table, para. .29
Control narratives Narratives describe intent ("access is reviewed regularly") in terms an auditor cannot test Narratives state who performs the control, what is done, when, how, the evidence produced and how exceptions are handled TSP 100, para. .01 (design and operating effectiveness)
Privacy Staff apply all privacy points of focus regardless of the organization's role Staff determine whether the organization acts as a data controller, a data processor or both, and read the [C] and [P] markers accordingly TSP 100, privacy criteria, fn. 21

The content gap analysis points the same way. The earlier draft summarized each Common Criterion in one or two lines without its points of focus, omitted the "to meet the entity's objectives" interpretation, and tested the seven risk significance factors of CC3.2 without listing them. Material of this kind leaves learners dependent on secondhand summaries, a plausible source of the misconceptions above.

3. Training and non-training causes

Training addresses causes in knowledge and skill. Problems of tooling and ownership require other remedies, so the analysis treats the two groups separately.

Causes addressable by training

  • Limited knowledge of the authority, structure and conventions of TSP 100.
  • Limited ability to relate service commitments and system requirements to scoping and interpretation.
  • Limited skill in mapping controls, writing testable narratives, judging evidence and conducting a gap assessment.

Environmental causes and recommendations

Environmental cause (assumed) Effect on performance Recommendation
No standard format for control narratives Narratives vary in completeness by author Adopt a control-narrative template built on the six elements taught in Module 8
Evidence held in personal drives, tickets and chat threads Evidence is incomplete or cannot be tied to a control and a period Establish a central evidence repository with a naming convention that records control ID, criterion and period
Unclear control ownership Recurring controls lapse during the Type 2 period Maintain a control ownership matrix and a compliance calendar for recurring controls
Service commitments made in contracts without GRC review Scope decisions rest on commitments that GRC staff have not seen Maintain a commitments register jointly with legal and sales
Compliance tooling that presents points of focus as checklist items Reinforces the checklist misconception Configure tooling around criteria, with points of focus shown as guidance

These recommendations would accompany the course. Without them, transfer of the skills it teaches is likely to be limited.

4. Organizational context

In a typical SaaS service organization, the request would come from the GRC or compliance lead, with sponsorship from the executive accountable for the SOC 2 program, often the chief information security officer. Demand often originates in sales, since enterprise customers commonly require a SOC 2 report before contract signature; the capstone scenario reflects this situation.

The training supports each stage of the SOC 2 cycle:

  • Readiness. A gap assessment, sometimes performed with a practitioner under the consulting standards, who develops findings and recommendations without expressing an opinion (TSP 100, para. .28).
  • Type 1. An examination of the design of controls at a point in time, dependent on accurate scoping, a complete system description and testable narratives.
  • Type 2. An examination of design and operating effectiveness over a period, dependent also on consistent operation of controls and evidence covering the period.
  • Annual renewal. Re-examination as scope, commitments, controls and staff change.

Errors carry observable costs. Untestable narratives produce rework during fieldwork; controls that do not operate as described produce exceptions and may require management responses in the report; scoping errors can require re-performance; and a delayed report can delay sales that depend on it. No organizational data were available to estimate these costs.

5. Learner analysis

The three profiles below are composites based on the role analysis and are presented as design assumptions.

Profile A: the new GRC analyst

  • Prior knowledge: General compliance concepts; little or no experience of TSP 100.
  • Needs: Orientation to the structure and vocabulary of the standard, then guided practice in scoping, mapping and narrative writing.
  • Motivation: Competence in a new role and credibility with auditors.
  • Constraints: Learns on the job, in fragmented study time.
  • Design implications: Vocabulary before explanation, worked examples before practice, and Module 9 as a lasting reference.

Profile B: the transferring professional

  • Prior knowledge: IT audit, internal audit or security operations; understands internal control or technical security, though the conventions of the TSC are new.
  • Needs: A clear account of what differs from prior frameworks: outcome-based design, the role of points of focus, the COSO alignment and the category-specific criteria.
  • Motivation: Efficient transfer of existing expertise; low tolerance for introductory material.
  • Constraints: Prior frameworks may interfere, for example by suggesting that the criteria prescribe controls.
  • Design implications: Free navigation, explicit treatment of misconceptions, and paragraph citations for verification.

Profile C: the control owner

  • Prior knowledge: Expert in engineering, IT or HR operations; limited knowledge of the criteria.
  • Needs: The criteria relevant to owned controls, the requirements of a testable narrative, and acceptable evidence.
  • Motivation: Fewer disruptive evidence requests; compliance is a secondary responsibility.
  • Constraints: Very limited time; likely to complete selected modules only.
  • Design implications: Self-contained modules (particularly Modules 5 and 8), role-based playbooks in Module 10, and a short job aid.

6. Job and task analysis

Frequency, criticality and difficulty ratings are analyst judgments from the role analysis, to be confirmed with practitioners. Module references follow the course structure.

Task Frequency Criticality Difficulty Module(s)

Write control narratives When controls are designed or changed High High M8 (8.1, 8.2, 8.4)

Tasks rated high in both criticality and difficulty receive guided practice with explanatory feedback; the remainder are supported mainly by worked examples and reference material.

7. Content analysis

TSP 100 contains 61 criteria: 33 Common Criteria and 28 category-specific criteria. The Common Criteria comprise 17 criteria in CC1–CC5, aligned to the 17 principles of the 2013 COSO framework, and 16 supplemental criteria in CC6–CC9 that supplement COSO principle 12 (TSP 100, para. .08). The category-specific criteria comprise 3 for availability, 5 for processing integrity, 2 for confidentiality and 18 for privacy, the last organized in eight series (P1–P8). Security uses the Common Criteria alone; each other category adds its own series to the Common Criteria (TSP 100, para. .10).

The principal points of difficulty are these:

  • Points of focus. They represent important characteristics of a criterion; their use does not require an assessment of whether each is addressed, and management may customize or add to them (TSP 100, paras. .04–.07).
  • Typographic conventions. COSO content appears in normal font, supplemental content in italics, and system-level content in bold italics (TSP 100, para. .29). The convention carries meaning and is easily overlooked.
  • Privacy markers. [C] marks a point of focus likely relevant to a data controller, [P] one likely relevant to a data processor. The markers indicate a typical allocation; the organization's facts govern (TSP 100, fn. 21).
  • Interpretation of objectives. In a SOC 2 engagement, "to meet the entity's objectives" refers to the service organization's commitments and system requirements, as the CC6.4 example shows (TSP 100, paras. .18–.24).
  • Applicability. A criterion for an in-scope category may be inapplicable only in limited circumstances (TSP 100, para. .11); when security is excluded, relevant aspects of the Common Criteria still apply (para. .15).
  • Volume. Some criteria carry many points of focus; CC8.1 lists more than a dozen, including baseline configuration, emergency changes and patch management.

These points imply a sequence: authority and the criteria and points of focus distinction (Module 1), the categories (Module 2), structure and conventions (Module 3), the criteria in detail (Modules 4–6), then application to scoping and gap assessment (Module 7) and to controls and evidence (Module 8), with reference and synthesis last (Modules 9–10). Module 8 depends on Module 3, since a learner who has not consolidated that distinction is likely to write narratives that conflate the two.

9. Constraints and delivery decision

The design operates within four constraints:

  • Delivery. Self-paced, with no dependency on a learning management system; distributed as a single deployable HTML file that also runs offline.
  • Accessibility. WCAG 2.1 Level AA as the target, including color contrast, semantic structure for screen readers, keyboard operation of activities, and definitions never available only on hover.
  • Time. Sessions of 30–60 minutes per module; approximately 10 hours for the full course, including practice and the optional capstone.
  • Working context. Study alongside the job, across several weeks, with later return to specific topics.

Instructor-led training would permit discussion of organization-specific cases, but it requires scheduling and a qualified facilitator for each cohort of new hires and leaves no lasting reference. A job aid alone would support experienced staff, but it cannot build the judgment that scoping, narrative writing and gap assessment require. Self-paced e-learning with embedded practice was selected because it fits short sessions, gives explanatory feedback on the high-difficulty tasks, allows control owners to study selectively, and remains available as a reference. A one- to two-page job aid is recommended as a complement, covering criteria counts by category, the six narrative elements, the evidence quality hierarchy and the gap assessment classifications.

10. Proposed success measures

The measures below are proposed for an organizational deployment, structured by Kirkpatrick's four levels. Baselines for Levels 3 and 4 would be established before release.

Level Proposed indicators Data source
1 · Reaction Average post-module confidence rating of at least 4.0 on a five-point scale; learner ratings of relevance to current tasks Post-module and end-of-course surveys
2 · Learning At least 3 of 5 correct on each module knowledge check; at least 11 of 15 on the optional capstone; per-section capstone results used to identify content needing reinforcement Embedded knowledge checks and capstone
3 · Behavior Control narratives accepted by the auditor without rework; scoping decisions that cite service commitments and system requirements; documented justification for any inapplicable criterion; evidence accepted at first submission Review of narratives and scoping documents; auditor request logs; manager checklist at 30, 60 and 90 days
4 · Results Fewer exceptions noted in tests of controls and fewer management-response items in the SOC 2 report; fewer auditor follow-up requests; shorter time from readiness to report issuance SOC 2 reports and fieldwork records compared across examination periods

Level 4 results depend on many factors besides training, including the changes recommended in Section 3, and should be reported as evidence of contribution.

11. Assumptions and validation plan

Assumption Validation method in a live engagement
The difficulty areas in Section 2 occur in the target organization Interviews with GRC leads; review of prior audit findings, exceptions and auditor requests
Learners have limited prior knowledge of TSP 100 conventions A short diagnostic quiz before release, drawn from the Module 1–3 knowledge checks
The three learner profiles describe the population Review of the GRC team roster and role descriptions with the sponsor; brief learner interviews
Task frequency, criticality and difficulty ratings are accurate Task rating exercise with two or three experienced practitioners
Learners can allocate 30–60 minutes per session Confirmation with managers; pilot completion times
The environmental causes in Section 3 are present Review of existing templates, evidence storage, ownership records and compliance tooling
Self-paced delivery without an LMS is acceptable to the organization Confirmation of hosting, completion tracking and accessibility requirements with IT and learning stakeholders

12. Recommendations

  1. Develop a ten-module self-paced course sequenced as in Section 7, with guided practice on high-criticality, high-difficulty tasks and an optional capstone.
  2. Cite TSP 100 by paragraph throughout, and design Module 9 and a job aid as working references.
  3. Present the environmental recommendations in Section 3 with the course.
  4. Validate the assumptions in Section 11 before release and collect the measures in Section 10 afterwards.

The course is organized around seven terminal objectives:

  1. TO1 (Understand): Explain the purpose, authority and structure of the Trust Services Criteria, including the distinction between criteria and points of focus and the conventions used in the document.
  2. TO2 (Analyze): Distinguish the five trust services categories and determine which apply to an organization, given its service commitments and system requirements.
  3. TO3 (Understand): Interpret the outcome required by each Common Criterion, including the COSO alignment of CC1–CC5 and the supplemental criteria in CC6–CC9.
  4. TO4 (Apply): Apply the category-specific criteria, including the privacy criteria and the distinction between data controllers and data processors, to determine the criteria in scope.
  5. TO5 (Apply): Prepare the scope of an engagement by defining the system boundary, identifying what the system description must address, and justifying any criterion that does not apply.
  6. TO6 (Create): Map controls to the criteria they support and write testable control narratives supported by appropriate evidence.
  7. TO7 (Evaluate): Evaluate an organization's readiness through a gap assessment and recommend remediation priorities.

This needs analysis was prepared for a portfolio project from primary source material and documented assumptions. It reports no client data. Designed and built by Tonja Ryan.

Case Study

Case Study

Project narrative

Trust Services Criteria for GRC Staff

A self-paced corporate compliance course

Role: Instructional Designer · Course Architect · UI/UX
Format: Self-paced, web-delivered, 10 modules
Source material: AICPA Trust Services Criteria (75-page PDF, 2017 with 2022 revisions)
Audience: Governance, Risk, and Compliance (GRC) professionals at SaaS service organizations
Deliverable: 10 module HTML files and a consolidated single-file deployment (621 KB)

At a glance

A corporate compliance course that presents a dense 75-page AICPA standard as a self-paced, interactive program for GRC professionals who prepare for or maintain SOC 2 examinations. The course uses a custom design system and fourteen engagement types, cites its content to the source by paragraph, and closes with an optional capstone scenario for application-level practice.

The problem

GRC professionals are expected to be fluent in the Trust Services Criteria, the AICPA standard that underlies every SOC 2 report, yet the source document is difficult to use. It comprises seventy-five pages of legalistic prose, sixty-one numbered criteria, eight series of points of focus, eight glossary categories, and a privacy section that uses shorthand markers ([P], [C], [P][C]) whose meaning is rarely explained to readers.

In practice, new GRC hires either spend weeks reading the PDF and emerge with an incomplete understanding, or they bypass the source and acquire misconceptions from secondhand summaries, which are often inaccurate. Audit firms, training vendors, and certification programs charge thousands of dollars per seat for content that amounts to a careful reading of one freely available document.

The project aimed to respect the authority of the source material while making it usable: a course that a learner could complete in a focused workweek and finish with practitioner-level fluency.

Audience analysis

A learner profile was developed before any screens were designed:

  • Role: Mid-career GRC professional, often newly assigned to SOC 2 oversight after working in adjacent compliance, IT audit, or security operations
  • Experience: Familiar with the language of internal controls but new to the specific TSC structure
  • Time available: 30–60 minutes per session, 5–10 sessions to course completion
  • Working context: Learners take the course while performing the job, so it must also serve as an ongoing working reference
  • Cognitive load: High existing demands; training that requires intensive memorization is impractical
  • Stakes: A misinterpreted criterion or a vague control narrative becomes an audit finding with a cost to the business
  • Motivation: Competence sufficient for the learner's work to withstand auditor review

The profile informed three foundational decisions:

  1. Design for use after the course ends. Module 9 (Glossary & References) was scoped from the start as a permanent working tool.
  2. Anchor every claim to the PDF source. Learners need assurance that the content reflects the standard itself. Page numbers and paragraph references appear throughout.
  3. Pace for cognitive realism. Each module corresponds to one focused learning session, and no module approaches four hours in length. Completion of every interactive element is not required, and exploration is encouraged.

Goals and learning objectives

The course has three meta-goals, mapped to a Bloom's taxonomy progression:

Meta-goal Bloom's level Module range
Recognize and recall the structure of the TSC Remember / Understand M1–M3
Apply the criteria to working scenarios Apply / Analyze M4–M8
Synthesize learning into job-applicable judgment Evaluate / Create M7, M8, M10

Module-level objectives were written as observable behaviors, for example "Distinguish criteria from points of focus" and "Construct a six-element control narrative." None are framed as passive exposure outcomes.

Design approach: key decisions

Decision 1 · Outcome-based vs. compliance-checklist framing

The source frames the TSC as outcome-based (TSP 100, para. .03): "the trust services criteria set forth the outcomes that an entity's controls should ordinarily meet... regardless of the specific controls implemented by management." This principle anchors Module 1 and is reinforced in Module 8, where learners build controls, and in Module 10, where it appears as one of five mental models. The most common GRC misconception, that SOC 2 is a checklist, is raised and corrected on the first screen of section 1.1.

Decision 2 · Fidelity to the source text

Compliance training in this domain often resembles marketing copy or vendor sales material. The course was written from the source text outward, with careful paraphrase and paragraph citations. Each direct quotation appears with its paragraph reference. This approach builds credibility with a skeptical professional audience and allows learners to use the course as a citable reference.

Decision 3 · Engagement variety as a cognitive load tool

Fourteen interaction types appear across the ten modules: click-to-reveal, sorting (5-bucket and 2×2), scenario decisions, hotspot identification, fill-in-the-blank, tier sort, accordion, matching, pipeline diagrams, timelines, searchable glossary, flashcards, tabs, and multiple choice. Each type was selected to match a specific cognitive task. Sorting reinforces categorical recognition, hotspots train pattern-matching, scenario decisions develop judgment, and flashcards support durable recall. The full mapping is documented in learning-design.md.

Decision 4 · Optional capstone, mandatory mental models

The original Module 10 outline made the 15-question MeridianHR capstone scenario a condition of course completion. Following the audience analysis, this arrangement was inverted. The mental models, the role-based corporate playbooks, and the future-paths section became the core of M10. The capstone moved to a clearly marked "Optional" section, with a "Skip to course wrap" link that scrolls to the closing section. A working professional may not have time for a 15-question exercise on a first pass, and withholding completion until the learner takes an optional test would create resistance that the course is designed to avoid.

Decision 5 · Reference-grade Module 9

Module 9 is the only module without a knowledge check. It contains a 93-term searchable glossary with category tabs and source attribution badges (PDF or Practice), three quick-lookup tables, six source-document cards, and an 18-card flashcard self-quiz. Reading the AICPA glossary verbatim and verifying every PDF term against the draft took longer than building any other section. The resulting reference is usable on the job, which the audience analysis identified as a primary need.

Solution overview

Architecture
- 10 standalone HTML module files (M1–M10) and an index/home page
- A consolidated tsc-training.html (621 KB) that hash-routes between modules in a single file
- Total course content: ~50,000 words of curriculum, 14 engagement types, 61 criteria covered, 93 glossary terms

Module flow
1. Foundations & Context
2. The Five Trust Services Categories
3. How Criteria Are Organized
4. Common Criteria CC1–CC5 (COSO-aligned core)
5. Common Criteria CC6–CC9 (security-specific layer)
6. Category-Specific Criteria (the 28 Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, and Privacy criteria)
7. Applying the Criteria (scoping, system boundaries, gap assessments)
8. From Criteria to Controls (six-element narratives, control types, evidence quality)
9. Glossary & References (working reference)
10. Synthesis & Capstone (mental models, corporate playbooks, optional capstone)

Design system
- A design system built on Google Material Design 3, with color roles generated from the author's brand palette and consistent container colors, icons and labels that distinguish types of learning content
- A lesson-by-lesson structure: each lesson moves from a plain-language orientation and key terms through explanation and a worked example to an activity and a checkpoint
- Material Symbols icons in place of emoji, for consistent visual treatment
- Component library documented in design-system.md

Assessment
- Five-question knowledge checks at the end of M1–M8 (formative)
- Self-quiz flashcards in M9 (no scoring; recall practice)
- Optional 15-question capstone in M10 with a per-section breakdown on completion (summative)
- Knowledge check explanations are full-paragraph rationales, written to extend learning at the point of assessment

Outcomes

For the learner
- Working understanding of all 61 criteria after course completion
- Ability to read and interpret the TSC document directly without secondhand reference
- Specific next-day actions through the role-based playbooks (first SOC 2 preparation, annual cycle, vendor review, stakeholder translation, first 30 days in a new GRC role)

Validation approach (planned, not yet executed)

Development is complete; the next phase is a structured pilot evaluation. The Kirkpatrick four-level plan in learning-design.md specifies the measures at each level (reaction, learning, behavior, and results) and how the resulting data would inform further iteration.

Lessons learned and iteration

Iteration 1: Visual breakage at scale

A first-pass review identified two design issues that had not appeared during development. Small fixed-size badges in the M1 engagement-type cards compressed multi-word labels until they were unreadable, and the sort-game tiles used pill-shaped containers (border-radius: 999px) that rendered 70-character sentences as elongated ovals. Both fixes were simple (60×48 badges, 12px border-radius), but the lesson was structural: in any course with variable-length user-generated or domain-driven content, fixed dimensions and pill containers fail. Flexible sizing with rounded rectangles was adopted wherever content length varied.

Iteration 2: A class-name collision in the consolidator

The consolidated single-file deployment merges module-specific CSS into a global stylesheet. Module 7 had its own .sort-item rule, correctly scoped for its short labels, but in the consolidated deployment that rule overrode the Module 1 rule and silently reversed the Iteration 1 fix. The M7 classes were therefore namespaced as .m7-sort-item-*. Lesson: when modules are designed in isolation and deployed together, CSS scoping must be defensive from the start. A consolidator rebuild script and a verification harness now check for class collisions.

Iteration 3: PDF coverage gap analysis

A late-stage audit cross-referenced every numbered paragraph in the PDF (.01 through .29) against the course content using a coverage matrix. The audit identified two content gaps. The foundational outcome principle (TSP 100, para. .03) appeared in M8 and M10 but was not anchored in M1, where learners first encounter the framework. The explicit statement that Common Criteria are not duplicated when categories are added was absent from M3, where learners first perform that calculation. Both gaps were closed with key-concept callouts that cite the source paragraph directly. Lesson: keyword-based coverage checks produce false negatives when a concept is paraphrased differently across modules. Their results are most useful as a prompt for manual review and should not be treated as conclusive.

Iteration 4: Three additional source anchors

A second, more detailed PDF audit added three source-anchored callouts: TSP 100, paras. .05 and .07 (points of focus are not mandatory) in M3, and para. .25 (the SSAE and AT-C 105/205/215 attestation framework) in M1. It also confirmed that para. .15 (the case in which security is not in scope) was already covered in M7, in wording the audit script had not searched for. Lesson: each audit pass surfaces issues the previous pass missed, and a third review is seldom wasted.

Changes for future projects

  • Pilot earlier. All ten modules were written before the first round of structured review. A single learner working through M1 in the first week would have identified the badge sizing issue.
  • Plan the assessment strategy alongside the content. The Kirkpatrick framework was applied retrospectively. Reaction, learning, behavior, and results metrics should be defined during the design phase.
  • Maintain an accessibility checklist from the outset. The accessibility considerations document was written after the course was complete. Some choices (color contrast, semantic HTML structure for screen readers) would have been easier to address if checked iteratively.

Project artifacts

  • The course: tsc-training.html (consolidated, 621 KB) and 11 individual module files
  • Source content: tsc-training-content.md (full prose curriculum)
  • Methodology: learning-design.md (Bloom's taxonomy, engagement matrix, Kirkpatrick assessment plan)
  • Design system: design-system.md (typography, color, components, accessibility)
  • Portfolio cover: portfolio-cover.html (entry point for the portfolio)
  • Source PDF: AICPA TSP Section 100, 2017, with revised points of focus (2022)

Learning Design Methodology

TSC for GRC Staff: instructional architecture, framework alignment, and assessment plan

This document sets out the rationale for the course's instructional decisions and relates each decision to an established framework. It accompanies the course and the project case study.

1 · Bloom's Taxonomy alignment

The course moves learners through the six cognitive levels of the revised Bloom's taxonomy (Anderson & Krathwohl, 2001). Module objectives are written as observable behaviors at the targeted level.

Cognitive progression across the course

Phase Modules Bloom's level Learner can...
Foundation M1, M2, M3 Remember · Understand Define key terms, recognize the structure of the TSC, distinguish criteria from points of focus
Knowledge building M4, M5, M6 Understand · Apply Explain each criterion series, identify which apply to a given category, interpret point-of-focus markers
Application M7, M8 Apply · Analyze Scope an engagement, draft a testable control narrative, classify control types, evaluate evidence quality
Synthesis M10 Evaluate · Create Apply the criteria to a novel scenario, construct role-specific implementation plans, defend scoping decisions
Reference M9 Remember (retrieval) Locate definitions, cross-reference criteria, find source documents on demand

Module-level objectives mapped to Bloom's

Module Sample objective Bloom's level Verified by
M1: Foundations "Identify the AICPA's role in publishing the TSC and contrast outcome-based vs. checklist approaches" Understand KC question 1.1, mental model #2 in M10
M2: Categories "Distinguish the five trust services categories and select which apply to a given organization" Apply KC question 2.4, scoping activity in M7
M3: Structure "Differentiate criteria from points of focus and recognize the COSO alignment of CC1–CC5" Analyze KC question 3.2, classification activity in M1.3
M4: CC1–CC5 "Map each Common Criterion CC1–CC5 to its COSO principle" Apply KC question 4.3
M5: CC6–CC9 "Identify the operational pipeline (access, ops, change, vendor) addressed by each supplemental CC series" Apply Matching activity in M5.3, KC question 5.4
M6: Category-specific "Determine the total number of criteria for any combination of trust services categories in scope" Apply Scope calculator in M6.5, capstone Q4
M7: Applying "Conduct a defensible scoping decision and identify limited-circumstances N/A exceptions" Evaluate Scoping activity, capstone Section 1
M8: Controls "Construct a six-element control narrative and classify it by control type and evidence quality" Create · Evaluate Fill-in-the-blank narrative builder, capstone Section 3
M9: Reference "Locate and apply definitions, source documents, and quick-reference math on demand" Remember (retrieval) Searchable glossary, quick-lookup tables
M10: Synthesis "Apply the full course to a corporate situation matching the learner's role" Evaluate · Create Role-based playbooks, optional capstone

Sequencing rationale

Module 8 (control narratives) depends on Module 3 (criteria and points of focus). A learner who attempts Module 8 without having consolidated Module 3 tends to write narratives that conflate criteria with points of focus, a pattern that also recurs in audit findings. The Bloom's progression therefore serves as the course's dependency structure, and modules cite earlier modules explicitly where they build on prior cognitive work.

Lesson architecture

Each module is presented one lesson at a time. A stepper at the top of the module shows the learner's position and allows movement to any lesson, and Back and Next controls close each lesson. Every lesson follows the same sequence: a short orientation in plain terms; the key vocabulary for the lesson; the core explanation, with the relevant source text from TSP 100; a worked example set at a fictional company; an interactive activity; and a one-question checkpoint with immediate feedback.

The sequence draws on several established findings. Presenting one lesson per screen applies Mayer's segmenting principle and reduces extraneous load, since the learner does not have to hold an entire module in view or locate a stopping point within a long page. Introducing vocabulary before the explanation applies the pre-training principle: learners who already know the names and meanings of the main terms can direct more capacity to the relationships between them. Consistent color coding of each lesson component applies the signaling principle, so that orientation, vocabulary, examples, activities and checkpoints are identifiable before they are read. Placing a worked example before the activity reflects the worked-example effect in cognitive load theory, which is strongest for novices, and much of the audience is new to SOC 2. The closing checkpoint provides retrieval practice (Roediger & Karpicke, 2006); a learner who answers incorrectly sees an explanation and may try again until the correct answer is identified.

Practice formats and checkpoint variation

Every lesson contains at least one activity that requires the learner to make a decision, and the checkpoints vary in format so that the end of each lesson does not become predictable. Four practice formats supplement the original activities, each chosen for a distinct cognitive task: classification for discriminating between related concepts (for example, a criterion and a point of focus), sequencing for processes with a fixed order (for example, the access lifecycle or an evidence-sampling procedure), highlighting for locating relevant language within an authentic artifact such as a control narrative or a system description, and statement completion for precise terminology and counts. Across the ten modules, fewer than a third of checkpoints are multiple choice.

The design deliberately excludes gamification. There are no points, timers or badges. Feedback is explanatory: each misplaced item or unsuitable selection displays the reason it does not fit, and the learner may revise and check again. This follows the evidence that elaborated feedback supports learning more than knowledge of results alone, and it keeps the emphasis on understanding the criteria.

2 · Engagement type rationale matrix

The course uses fourteen distinct interaction types. Each type was selected for a specific cognitive purpose. Where applicable, the choice is grounded in Mayer's principles of multimedia learning (Mayer, 2009) or in alignment with a level of Bloom's taxonomy.

Engagement type Where used Cognitive purpose Framework alignment
Click-to-reveal cards M1, M2, M3, M5, M7, M8, M9, M10 Progressive disclosure; reduces extraneous cognitive load on first encounter Mayer: segmenting principle
Pull quotes / key-concept callouts All modules Anchor a concept in the source text before the learner proceeds Mayer: signaling principle
Classification sort (five categories) M5, M7 Build categorical recognition of which criterion belongs to which series Bloom: Apply / Analyze
Classification sort (2×2 matrix) M8 Train two-dimensional classification (manual/auto × preventive/detective) Bloom: Apply / Analyze
Scenario decision M5, M7 Practice professional judgment in realistic, consequential situations Bloom: Evaluate
Multiple choice (knowledge check) M1–M8, M10 Formative assessment with explanatory feedback on every item Mayer: feedback principle
True / false M2 Surface and correct misconceptions efficiently Bloom: Understand
Accordion (extended detail) M6 Provide optional depth without lengthening the primary sequence Mayer: pre-training principle
Matching M5 Build associations between controls and criteria Bloom: Understand / Apply
Pipeline / timeline M5, M6, M10 Represent sequential and process relationships graphically Mayer: spatial contiguity principle
Hotspot identification M8 Train pattern recognition in long-form text (six-element narrative parts) Bloom: Analyze
Fill-in-the-blank M8 Practice constructive recall in narrative contexts Bloom: Apply / Create
Tier sort M8 Calibrate evidence quality judgment (high/medium/low) Bloom: Evaluate
Searchable glossary + filter tabs M9 Support on-demand retrieval during applied work Bloom: Remember (retrieval)
Flashcards (3D flip) M9 Strengthen long-term recall of core terminology Retrieval practice; testing effect (Roediger & Karpicke, 2006)
Tab-based playbooks M10 Permit role-based selection of content without requiring a fixed sequence Mayer: personalization principle

Number of engagement types

A course that relies on a single engagement type becomes predictable, and learner attention declines. A course that uses too many imposes a new interface demand each time the format changes. Fourteen types across ten modules averages 1.4 interaction types per module, which offers enough variety to sustain attention while allowing learners to adapt quickly to each format. Each module uses 2–3 engagement types selected to match its cognitive task.

3 · Application of Mayer's principles of multimedia learning

Richard Mayer's twelve principles informed the following design decisions.

Principle How the course applies it
Coherence The course contains no decorative emoji or unrelated stock imagery; Material Symbols icons, each paired with a text label, are used in their place. Each visual element carries instructional content.
Signaling Each kind of lesson content has a consistent label, icon and Material Design 3 container: a surface-container card for orientation, a secondary-container card for the key-terms panel, an outlined card for worked examples, tertiary-container cards for principle statements, and elevated cards for activities and checkpoints. Lesson numbers and the lesson stepper serve as navigational anchors.
Redundancy Written narrative is paired with diagrams, and on-screen text is not duplicated by audio narration. Because reading speed varies, learners control their own pace.
Spatial contiguity Point-of-focus examples appear directly beside their parent criterion on the same screen. Glossary definitions appear inline and are never available only on hover.
Segmenting Each module is divided into lessons presented one per screen, and reveal interactions allow learners to control the depth of treatment.
Pre-training Each lesson introduces its key terms before the core explanation, and M9 (Glossary) is structured so that learners may review terminology before beginning the more advanced modules.
Personalization The role-based playbooks in M10 address the learner's situation directly, for example a new member of a GRC team or a practitioner preparing for a first SOC 2 examination. Activity instructions address the learner in the second person.
Feedback Each knowledge-check explanation is a full paragraph that teaches the underlying concept in addition to stating whether the response is correct.

4 · Evaluation strategy: Kirkpatrick's Four Levels

Donald Kirkpatrick's four-level model (Kirkpatrick & Kirkpatrick, 2016) frames how this course would be evaluated in an organizational deployment. The course is complete; the evaluation plan describes the subsequent phase.

Level 1 · Reaction

Question: Did learners find the course useful and engaging?

Method: A post-module micro-survey (3 questions, approximately 30 seconds) and an end-of-course survey (10 questions, approximately 3 minutes).

Sample items:
- "On a scale of 1–5, how confident do you feel applying this module's content tomorrow?"
- "Which engagement type in this module helped you most?"
- "What part of the course was most/least useful?"

Decision threshold: Each module should achieve an average confidence rating of at least 4.0, and fewer than 10% of learners should report it as "least useful." A module that misses either threshold is revised.

Level 2 · Learning

Question: Did learners acquire the intended knowledge and skills?

Method: Built into the course as formative assessment (knowledge checks M1–M8) and summative assessment (M10 optional capstone, 15 questions).

Pass thresholds:
- Knowledge checks: ≥3 of 5 correct per module signals adequate retention
- Capstone: ≥11 of 15 (73%) for practitioner-level fluency
- Per-section breakdown in capstone identifies which content areas need reinforcement

Status: These mechanisms are already operational in the course. Aggregation of results across cohorts is the next step.

Level 3 · Behavior

Question: Are learners applying the course content on the job?

Method: Manager surveys at 30, 60, and 90 days after course completion, supplemented by learner self-assessment. A behavioral checklist covers seven observable on-the-job behaviors:

  1. Cites paragraph numbers when referencing the TSC standard
  2. Distinguishes criteria from points of focus in conversation
  3. Writes control narratives addressing all six elements (Who/What/When/How/Evidence/Exception)
  4. Recommends scope decisions citing customer commitments and system requirements
  5. Identifies CUECs and subservice organizations correctly when reviewing vendor SOC 2 reports
  6. Explains TSC concepts clearly to non-GRC stakeholders (engineering, sales, leadership)
  7. Maintains a quarterly cadence on access reviews and vendor risk reviews

Decision threshold: Observation of at least 5 of the 7 behaviors at 90 days indicates that the course is producing behavioral change.

Level 4 · Results

Question: Is the course contributing to measurable organizational outcomes?

Method: Six-month and twelve-month organizational metrics tracked alongside cohort completion.

Candidate metrics:

Metric Pre-course baseline 12-month target
Audit findings on control-narrative clarity TBD -50%
Time from audit kickoff to evidence completion TBD -25%
GRC team time spent on stakeholder questions about TSC basics TBD -40%
Confidence ratings from auditors on control walkthroughs TBD +1.0 (5-point scale)
Days to onboard a new GRC team member to SOC 2 program 60 days 30 days

Limitation: Attribution at Level 4 is difficult because the course is one of several inputs to any organizational outcome. Results-level findings should therefore be reported as evidence of contribution; they do not support causal claims.

5 · Audience-specific design choices

The audience analysis (working professionals, 30–60 minute sessions, post-course reference need) informed the following design decisions.

Audience need Course design response
Use of the course as an on-the-job reference Module 9 designed as a standalone working reference; consolidated single-file deployment for offline access
Limited time for introductory or review material Recap and introductory filler removed; each module opens with new material; principle callouts foreground the central idea
Skepticism toward compliance training Every claim anchored to the source with TSP 100 paragraph citations; marketing language excluded; learners addressed as professional peers
Return to specific topics weeks after initial study Hash-based routing in the consolidated file; module navigation; deep-linkable sections
Completion across multiple sessions No completion gates; optional capstone; progress indicators per module
Fragmented study time Modules average 30–45 minutes; each lesson is a natural stopping point, and the lesson stepper shows the learner's position on return

6 · ADDIE phase summary

Phase Activities
Analysis Audience profile (corporate GRC professionals); needs analysis (existing alternatives are dense, vendor-driven, or expensive); content analysis of source PDF (75 pages, 26 paragraphs, 61 criteria, 8 glossary categories)
Design Module structure (10 modules across 5 phases); learning objective drafting (Bloom's-aligned); design system definition (Material Design 3 foundation, color roles generated from the brand palette, typography, components); engagement type planning (14 types selected for cognitive purpose)
Development Iterative module build (M1 through M10); custom HTML/CSS/JS; SVG icon library (~31 icons); knowledge checks; capstone scenario design
Implementation Consolidated single-file deployment and standalone module files; portfolio cover page; documentation (case study, this document, design system)
Evaluation Internal accuracy audits (PDF coverage matrix, two passes); design review (screenshot-based inspection for rendering defects); Kirkpatrick four-level plan documented for future deployment

References

  • Anderson, L. W., & Krathwohl, D. R. (2001). A Taxonomy for Learning, Teaching, and Assessing: A Revision of Bloom's Taxonomy of Educational Objectives. Longman.
  • Kirkpatrick, J. D., & Kirkpatrick, W. K. (2016). Kirkpatrick's Four Levels of Training Evaluation. ATD Press.
  • Mayer, R. E. (2009). Multimedia Learning (2nd ed.). Cambridge University Press.
  • Roediger, H. L., & Karpicke, J. D. (2006). The Power of Testing Memory: Basic Research and Implications for Educational Practice. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 1(3), 181–210.
  • AICPA Assurance Services Executive Committee. (2022). TSP Section 100: 2017 Trust Services Criteria with Revised Points of Focus, 2022. American Institute of Certified Public Accountants.

Design System

Visual language · components · accessibility

Design System

TSC for GRC Staff: visual language, components and accessibility

This document records the visual decisions behind the course so that later revisions remain consistent, so that collaborators have a single reference, and so that reviewers can see the reasoning behind each choice.

1 · Foundation

The course adopts Google's Material Design 3 (M3) as its foundational design system. The interface is built from M3 system tokens for color, typography, shape, elevation and state, and each course component is mapped to a documented M3 component.

Rationale. An established, documented and accessible system gives the course predictable interaction patterns, color roles with tested contrast relationships, and a shared vocabulary for collaborators and developers. A developer who extends the course can identify a component as a filled tonal button or an input chip and consult the M3 specification for its expected behavior. Learners, many of whom use Material-based products daily, meet controls whose appearance indicates what they do.

Brand identity within the framework. The author's brand palette supplies the source colors from which the M3 color roles are generated:

Source color Hex Generates
Midnight #013D5A Primary palette
Herb #708C69 Secondary palette and the extended success color
Marigold #F4A258 Tertiary palette
Lionsmane #FCF3E3 Hue of the neutral and neutral-variant palettes
Celeste #BDD3CE A supplementary tonal palette held in reserve (--md-ext-celeste-container); no current component uses it

The course therefore keeps its identity while every surface, text color and state follows M3 rules.

Guiding principles:

  1. Roles before colors. Components reference color roles (primary, secondary container, surface container high) and never raw hex values. A change to the source colors regenerates every role consistently.
  2. A consistent lesson sequence. Every lesson presents its components in the same order and with the same treatment, so the learner's attention goes to the content and the layout does not have to be relearned on each screen.
  3. Elevation indicates interaction. Elevated cards are reserved for surfaces the learner manipulates (activities, checkpoints, knowledge checks). Expository content sits on filled or outlined cards at level 0.
  4. Label, icon and color together. Each content type is identified by a text label and a Material Symbol as well as by its container color, so that no meaning depends on color alone.

2 · Color

Generation

The color roles were generated with Google's material-color-utilities library (v0.3.0) using a DynamicScheme with the tonal-spot variant, a light scheme and the standard contrast level. Each palette was built from its source color:

  • Primary from Midnight, secondary from Herb and tertiary from Marigold, each as a full tonal palette
  • Neutral and neutral variant from the hue of Lionsmane at low chroma (6 and 10 respectively), which gives the surfaces a warm cast without visible tinting
  • Error from the M3 baseline error palette

The primary role is pinned to the exact Midnight value. This is equivalent to the color-match option in Material Theme Builder, and it ensures that the brand color appears unaltered on primary actions. All other roles are taken directly from the generated scheme.

Color roles

Role Hex Use in the course

on-primary #FFFFFF Text and icons on primary
primary-container #C9E6FF Lesson headers (alternating with secondary container), the course-plan introduction, objective and sequence-step numerals, the matching-activity label, the navigation drawer toggle, text selection
on-primary-container #194B69 Text on primary container

secondary-container #CCEBC2 The active indicator in the navigation drawer, alternate lesson headers, the key-terms panel, filled tonal buttons, selected chips and segments, activity and practice labels, the linear progress track

tertiary-container #FFDCC2 Principle and practice-note cards, the worked-example label, the scenario-activity label, selected phrases in highlight activities, the higher Bloom's levels on objective cards
on-tertiary-container #6D3A00 Text on tertiary container
error #BA1A1A The incorrect-answer icon and the border of an incorrect cloze blank
error-container #FFDAD6 Incorrect answers, incorrect placements and incorrect-answer feedback

Extended color: success

M3 defines no role for a correct answer, so the course adds a custom extended color named success, harmonized from Herb: success #4B6545 with success-container #CCEBC2 and on-success-container #082007. Correct answers, correct placements and correct-answer feedback use the success container; the check icon uses the success color. Because success is derived from the same Herb palette as the secondary role, its tones coincide with the secondary values, and a correct answer is identified by its icon and feedback text as well as by its fill. Incorrect answers use the error roles.

Contrast

Contrast ratios were computed from the generated hex values with the WCAG 2.x relative-luminance formula.

Pairing Ratio WCAG level
on-surface on surface 16.3:1 AAA
on-primary on primary 11.6:1 AAA
on-surface-variant on surface 8.9:1 AAA
on-primary-container on primary-container 7.2:1 AAA
on-secondary-container on secondary-container 7.2:1 AAA
on-tertiary-container on tertiary-container 7.2:1 AAA
on-error-container on error-container 7.2:1 AAA
on-success-container on success-container 13.3:1 AAA
secondary (focus indicator) on surface 6.1:1 Exceeds the 3:1 non-text threshold
outline on surface 4.3:1 Exceeds the 3:1 non-text threshold

The uniform 7.2:1 ratio across container pairings follows from the tonal-spot scheme, which places every container at tone 90 and its on-color at tone 30 of the same palette.

3 · Typography

The course uses the M3 type scale with three typefaces assigned through reference tokens.

Token Family Role
--md-ref-typeface-brand Roboto Flex Display, headline and title large roles
--md-ref-typeface-plain Roboto Title medium, body and label roles
--md-ref-typeface-mono Roboto Mono Criterion IDs, lesson numbers, numerals, counts and scores

The monospaced face carries reference information. Criterion IDs such as CC6.1, lesson numbers, objective codes, sequence numerals and knowledge-check scores are set in Roboto Mono so that identifiers read as identifiers and align consistently. Mono is not used for running text or buttons.

Type roles in use

Role Size / line-height Where it appears

Headline large 32px / 40px Lesson header titles, the course-plan introduction title
Headline medium 28px / 36px Knowledge-check titles
Headline small 24px / 32px Learning-objectives heading, course-plan section headings
Title large 22px / 28px Activity, practice and worked-example titles; module navigation targets; the course name in the top app bar and drawer
Title medium 16px / 24px, weight 500 Checkpoint questions, category-bin headings, sequencing-map module titles
Body large 16px / 24px (1.65 in reading content) Reading content, "In plain terms" text, objective statements
Body medium 14px / 20px Activity prompts, term definitions, feedback panels, course-plan lead text

Headings use weight 400 in Roboto Flex, in keeping with the M3 baseline, with weight 500 for h3 and below. Title medium follows the M3 baseline in using the plain typeface.

4 · Shape

Corner radii follow the M3 shape scale.

Token Radius Components
Extra small 4px Cloze blanks (outlined menu fields), highlighted phrases
Small 8px Assist, input and filter chips; content labels; lesson-number and objective-code chips; knowledge-check numerals
Medium 12px Outlined cards (worked examples, module navigation, accordions), context and principle cards, selection list items, feedback panels, item banks and bins, sequence steps
Large 16px Filled cards ("In plain terms", key terms), activity and practice cards, checkpoints, the drawer toggle, the modal drawer's trailing edge
Extra large 28px Lesson headers, the course-plan introduction, knowledge checks, the completion panel
Full 9999px All buttons, drawer items and their active indicator, segmented buttons, the search bar

5 · Elevation and state

Elevation

The course uses the M3 shadow specifications for elevation levels 0 to 4.

  • Level 0: all expository content, filled and outlined cards at rest, the top app bar and the standard drawer
  • Level 1: activity and practice cards, checkpoints and knowledge checks; the hover state of filled and tonal buttons and of outlined cards; an expanded key-term chip; a selected input chip; the modal drawer on narrow screens
  • Level 2: defined in the token set and not currently assigned
  • Level 3: the navigation drawer toggle shown below 900px
  • Level 4: an item while it is being dragged

State layers

Interactive states follow the M3 state-layer model: a translucent layer of the content color is laid over the container. The opacities are defined as tokens (hover 8%, focus 10%, pressed 10%, dragged 16%) and applied with CSS color-mix(), for example color-mix(in srgb, var(--md-sys-color-on-surface) 8%, transparent) for the hover state of a drawer item or list item. On filled buttons the layer mixes the on-color into the container color. Disabled controls take on-surface at 12% for the container and 38% for the content, as M3 specifies.

6 · Iconography

Interface icons are drawn from Material Symbols Rounded, loaded as a variable icon font and rendered through ligatures (the icon name is written as text and the font substitutes the glyph). Icons render at 18 to 24px, with weight 400 and the outlined style at rest; the filled style marks the answer state after a choice is checked. Every icon accompanies a text label and is never the sole carrier of meaning.

Symbol Assigned to
lightbulb In plain terms
menu_book Key terms
work Example
task_alt Checkpoint
info Context
priority_high Principle and practice notes
drag_pan Classification activities
link Matching activities
account_tree Scenario activities
ink_highlighter Highlight activities

explore Exploration activities
psychology Reflection activities
format_list_numbered Sequence practice
drag_indicator The grip on every draggable item
radio_button_unchecked, check_circle, cancel Answer states: unanswered, correct and incorrect

Supporting symbols include expand_more and expand_less on expandable chips and list items, check on selected filter chips and segments, and arrow_upward and arrow_downward on reorder icon buttons. A small number of inline SVG illustrations remain within activity content in several modules; they are drawn in currentColor and therefore take the on-color of their container.

7 · Component mapping

Each course component is implemented as, or styled to the specification of, an M3 component.

Course component M3 component
Sidebar Navigation drawer: standard at desktop widths, modal below 900px; active indicator in secondary container
Top bar Small top app bar
Lesson stepper Primary tabs with a linear progress indicator
Begin, Next and Check Filled buttons
Back and secondary links Outlined buttons
Reveal actions Filled tonal buttons
Reorder arrows Icon buttons
Eyebrows and content labels Assist chips
Key terms and draggable items Input chips (key terms are expandable)
Glossary categories and playbook tabs Filter chips
Checklist versus Outcome toggle Segmented buttons
Glossary search Search bar
Cloze blanks Outlined menu (select) fields
Lesson header and course-plan introduction Filled cards in primary or secondary container
In plain terms Filled card (surface container highest)

8 · Lesson structure

Each module is presented one lesson at a time. The following components appear in every lesson, in this order.

Lesson stepper. A row of primary tabs, sticky beneath the top app bar at desktop widths and static below 900px. Above the tabs, a metadata line gives the module label in primary, the lesson count ("Lesson 2 of 5") and a 4px linear progress indicator with a primary fill on a secondary-container track. Each tab shows a mono lesson number, a truncated title and a small status dot; the active tab carries the primary active indicator and aria-current="step", and the dot of a visited lesson takes the secondary color. Selecting a tab opens that lesson.

Lesson header. A filled card with an extra-large corner, in primary container or secondary container, alternating from lesson to lesson so that adjacent lessons are visibly distinct. The alternation is positional and carries no semantic meaning. The title is set in headline large, beneath a small chip giving the lesson number in mono.

"In plain terms" card. A filled card in surface container highest, labeled with the lightbulb symbol. It states in plain language what the lesson covers before any regulatory text appears.

Key-terms panel. A filled card in secondary container, labeled with menu_book, holding a row of input chips. Selecting a chip expands it to the full width of the panel at level 1 and reveals the definition; opening one chip closes any other open chip in the same group. The chips are native <details> elements. At desktop widths the "In plain terms" card and the key-terms panel sit side by side in a 1.25:1 grid.

Explanation. Body text on the page surface, with context cards (surface container, info), source-text cards and principle or practice-note cards (tertiary container, priority_high) as the content requires. Source-text labels always give the paragraph reference, for example "Source text · TSP 100, para. .03".

Worked example. An outlined card labeled with work in tertiary container. It applies the lesson's concept to a fictional company, often as a numbered sequence.

Activity. The lesson's interactive exercise on an elevated card, labeled "Activity · Classification" or similar with the symbol for its kind.

Checkpoint. An elevated card in surface container low with a primary "Checkpoint" label (task_alt). It asks one question with three options presented as selection list items with radio indicators. Feedback is immediate: a correct choice takes the success container and a filled check_circle and closes the checkpoint; an incorrect choice takes the error container and a filled cancel and is disabled, so the learner may retry until the correct option is found. An explanatory sentence appears beneath the options in the matching container.

Lesson footer. Separated from the lesson by an outline-variant divider. An outlined Back button sits on the left and a filled Next button, naming the next lesson, on the right. On the final lesson, module navigation appears in place of further lessons.

Drag and drop

All classification, matching and sequencing activities accept pointer dragging with a mouse, a finger or a pen. Each draggable item is an input chip with a drag_indicator grip. While an item is dragged, a copy at elevation level 4 follows the pointer, the source item fades to 38% opacity, and the eligible destination shows a 2px primary outline with an 8% primary state layer. Every drag interaction has an equivalent select-then-place path: the learner selects an item (which takes secondary container at level 1), then selects its destination. Sequence steps can also be reordered with up and down icon buttons. Both alternatives are operable from the keyboard, so dragging is never required.

Practice formats

Four practice formats share one structure on an elevated card: a content label with the symbol for the format, a title in title large, an instruction in body medium, the task, a filled Check button and a feedback panel announced through aria-live.

  • Classification (drag_pan): items in a dashed item bank are sorted into outlined category bins.
  • Sequence (format_list_numbered): numbered steps, each a list item with a primary-container numeral, are reordered by dragging or with the arrow icon buttons.
  • Highlight (ink_highlighter): selectable phrases within a realistic passage take tertiary container when selected.
  • Complete the statement (edit_note): outlined menu fields set within a sentence.

After checking, each item takes the success or error container; incorrect items also carry a short explanation, and incorrectly highlighted phrases are struck through. Feedback explains each incorrect placement and allows another attempt; the course records no scores. When a practice block serves as the lesson checkpoint, it takes the checkpoint surface and primary label.

Other components

Knowledge check. An elevated card with an extra-large corner. Questions are separated by dividers and open with a mono numeral on a primary chip. Options are outlined list items that take secondary container when selected, success container when correct and error container when incorrect. Feedback appears in surface container as a full explanatory paragraph.

Learning objectives. An outlined card containing a divided list; each objective is numbered with a mono numeral in a primary-container circle.

Course plan. The course home presents an introduction in a primary-container filled card, objective cards in surface container low with assist chips for the objective code and Bloom's level, an alignment matrix in an outlined card, and a sequencing map in which each module is an expandable list item.

Reveal card, scenario decision, hotspot and flashcard. These original activities sit on elevated cards; their inner cards are outlined cards, and each reveal action is a filled tonal button that takes the success container once revealed.

9 · Layout

  • Navigation drawer: 280px wide at desktop widths; below 900px it becomes a 300px modal drawer opened by a toggle button, and the top app bar leaves room for that toggle
  • Maximum reading width: 720–800px for prose-heavy content
  • Card grids: two columns at desktop and one column on narrow screens; grid children may shrink and long words wrap so that columns stay within the viewport
  • Wide visualizations (timelines, scope tables, the alignment matrix): full container width up to 1100px; on screens narrower than 640px, tables scroll horizontally within their own container
  • Narrow screens: below 720px the lesson introduction stacks into one column; below 640px the page uses a 16px side gutter, card padding tightens to 20px by 16px, lesson tabs show only their numbers, and the Back and Next buttons span the full width
  • Spacing: a 4px base, with values such as 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28, 32 and 40px for padding and margins between components

10 · Accessibility

Measures in place

  • Color contrast: body text measures 16.3:1 on the page and secondary text 8.9:1; text on primary measures 11.6:1; every container pairing (primary, secondary, tertiary and error) measures 7.2:1, and text on the success container 13.3:1. All text pairings meet WCAG AAA. Outlines measure 4.3:1 against the page, above the 3:1 threshold for non-text contrast
  • Focus indicator: every focusable element shows a 3px outline in the secondary color with a 2px offset, measuring 6.1:1 against the page; text fields take a 2px primary border on focus
  • State without color dependence: answer states carry Material Symbols (check_circle, cancel) and explanatory text; incorrect checkpoint answers are disabled; incorrectly highlighted phrases are struck through; selected filter chips and segments carry a check; every lesson block and activity carries a text label with its icon
  • Feedback announcements: checkpoint, practice and knowledge-check feedback is written into containers with aria-live="polite", so screen readers announce the result of each attempt
  • Keyboard alternatives: every drag interaction has a select-then-place path, and sequences can be reordered with icon buttons
  • Reduced motion: under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, animations and transitions are reduced to an effectively instant duration and smooth scrolling is disabled
  • Semantic HTML: section headers use <h1>, <h2> and <h3>; lists use <ul> and <ol>; buttons use <button>; links use <a>; the course contains no <div onclick> patterns
  • Native disclosure: key-term chips and sequencing-map items are <details> elements, so expansion state is exposed to assistive technology without custom scripting
  • Icons: icon glyphs accompany visible text labels; inline SVG illustrations use aria-hidden="true" when paired with a label
  • Reading order and scaling: DOM order matches visual order, and sizes remain scalable with no container depending on fixed text dimensions

Outstanding work

  • Skip-to-content links: not yet implemented; they should be added so that keyboard users can bypass the navigation drawer

About this course

The Trust Services Criteria (TSC) form the foundation of SOC 2, SOC 3, and SOC for Cybersecurity examinations. Many compliance professionals nonetheless work with the criteria daily without a thorough understanding of how the criteria are structured, how they should be interpreted, or how they apply across engagement types.

This course provides that foundation. Its ten modules progress from foundational concepts (the nature and purpose of the TSC) through structural understanding (the organization of the criteria and their relationship to COSO) to applied evaluation (mapping criteria to controls and scoping engagements). The modules combine structured content with interactive exercises and knowledge checks.

Course format

Self-paced online learning, with applied exercises in every module.

10 Modules

Foundations through applied evaluation

~10 Hours

Approximate total course time, self-paced

Interactive

Sort exercises, scenarios, and knowledge checks

Capstone

Optional synthesis assessment in Module 10

Who this is for

This course is designed for professionals who work with the TSC in their day-to-day responsibilities at a service organization.

  • Compliance and GRC staff at service organizations
  • Internal audit teams supporting SOC engagements
  • Risk and security teams responsible for control evidence
  • Anyone preparing for or maintaining a SOC 2 program
