Module 1

Foundations & Context

This module establishes what the Trust Services Criteria are, why they exist, and the engagements in which they are used. Later modules build on this foundation.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this module
  • Explain what the Trust Services Criteria (TSC) are and why they exist
  • Distinguish outcome-based criteria from prescriptive control frameworks
  • Describe the relationship between criteria and points of focus
  • Identify the engagement types where the TSC is used
  • Recognize how the same criterion can be interpreted differently across engagement types
Module 1 · Begin
1.1

What problem does the TSC solve?

In plain terms

Companies that store or process data for their customers are often asked to prove that the data is protected. A common way to provide that proof is an independent examination by a certified public accountant (CPA), who then issues a report such as a SOC 2 report. The CPA needs a published benchmark to measure the company against, and the Trust Services Criteria (TSC) serve as that benchmark. This lesson explains why the TSC describes the outcomes that controls must achieve and leaves each company to choose its own controls. That idea shapes how GRC staff prepare for an audit and how they explain their organization's controls to an auditor.

Key terms
Control

A policy, procedure, or technical mechanism that an organization uses to address a risk. Requiring a second sign-in factor before an employee can reach customer data is one example.

Entity

The organization whose controls are being evaluated. TSP 100 uses the word broadly; a service organization undergoing a SOC 2 examination is one kind of entity.

Criteria

The benchmarks against which something is measured or evaluated. In this course the term refers to the Trust Services Criteria, which are statements of what an entity's controls should achieve. The singular is criterion.

Criterion reference (for example, CC6.1)

Each criterion has a reference number. CC stands for common criteria, the criteria shared by all five trust services categories (introduced in lesson 1.3). CC6.1 is the first criterion in the CC6 series, which addresses logical and physical access controls.

Context

An evaluation of whether an organization keeps its customers' data secure might begin with a checklist, as many compliance frameworks do. Organizations differ considerably, however. A small financial technology company faces different threats from those facing a global hospital network, and a checklist written to fit both tends to be either too generic to be meaningful or too extensive for any entity to satisfy in full.

The Trust Services Criteria address this problem by stating the outcomes an entity's controls must achieve. Each entity determines how to achieve those outcomes in light of its own circumstances.

Example

Two companies, one criterion

Northwind Payroll is a 40-person company that sells payroll software to small businesses. Criterion CC6.1 requires the entity to implement logical access security over protected information assets to protect them from security events. Northwind addresses that outcome with three controls:

  1. Every employee signs in through a single sign-on service that requires multifactor authentication.
  2. The production database accepts connections only from a restricted administrative network.
  3. Access to customer payroll data is limited to the support and engineering roles that need it.

A global bank evaluated against the same criterion would likely operate more numerous and more specialized controls, because its systems and threats differ. The auditor asks each company the same question: do the controls in place achieve the outcome CC6.1 describes, given this entity's risks? Neither company is measured against the other's set of controls.

Activity · Comparison

Two ways to evaluate controls

Select each button to compare the two approaches.

Prescriptive approach

  • Specifies exact controls every entity must implement
  • Scored simply, by whether each control is present
  • Assumes that all organizations face the same risks
  • Tends to be too generic for some entities and too prescriptive for others
  • Encourages treating compliance itself as the objective

Outcome-based approach

  • Specifies the outcomes that controls must achieve
  • Each entity decides which controls fit its environment
  • Applies to entities of any size, from small companies to global enterprises
  • Auditors evaluate whether the outcomes are met, whatever controls the entity has selected
  • Requires each organization to understand its own risks
Principle The TSC is outcome-based. It defines what controls must accomplish and leaves the selection of specific controls to the entity.
Source text · TSP 100, para. .03

Paragraph .03 states the principle directly: the trust services criteria set forth the outcomes an entity's controls should meet and are intended for evaluation and reporting regardless of the specific controls implemented by management. This distinguishes the TSC from process-and-control frameworks that mandate specific controls. Because each entity sets its own objectives, assesses its own risks, and selects its own controls, applying the criteria in actual situations requires judgment. The emphasis on judgment recurs in TSP 100, para. .07, and informs the remainder of the course.

Practice note: When an auditor asks how the entity meets CC6.1, the auditor is asking whether the outcome the criterion describes (protection of information assets through logical access security) is being achieved. GRC staff are responsible for articulating how the implemented controls achieve the outcomes the criteria require.

For this reason, the TSC is outcome-based

The TSC sets out the that an entity's controls should meet. When evaluating CC6.1 at Northwind Payroll, the auditor asks whether the controls that achieve the outcome the criterion describes.

1.2

Who issues the TSC and why it matters

In plain terms

An audit report is only as credible as the benchmark behind it. If each auditor wrote its own standards, a reader could not tell whether those standards were fair or compare one company's report with another's. The TSC is written by a committee of the AICPA, the professional body for certified public accountants in the United States, and that origin is what allows auditors and report readers to rely on it. This lesson covers who issues the criteria, the four tests that any criteria used by an auditor must pass, and how the TSC has been revised since 2017. The 2022 revision concerns points of focus, the supporting details beneath each criterion that lesson 1.3 explains.

Key terms
AICPA

The American Institute of Certified Public Accountants, the U.S. professional body for CPAs. It publishes the TSC and the attestation standards that CPAs follow when they report on an organization.

Suitable criteria

Criteria that are relevant, objective, measurable, and complete, as the attestation standards require. ASEC has concluded that the trust services criteria are suitable criteria (TSP 100, para. .26).

COSO

The Committee of Sponsoring Organizations of the Treadway Commission. Its internal control framework, revised in 2013, sets out 17 principles of internal control, and the TSC is aligned to those 17 principles.

Practitioner (service auditor)

The CPA who performs the engagement. The TSC document uses the term practitioner; the AICPA SOC 2 Guide uses service auditor for the same role in a SOC 2 examination.

Issuing Authority

The TSC is developed by the AICPA through its Assurance Services Executive Committee (ASEC). This origin gives the TSC formal standing under professional standards: an auditor who uses the TSC to form an opinion is applying criteria that the profession has formally recognized as appropriate.

The issuing body: The TSC is published by the AICPA (American Institute of Certified Public Accountants). It is developed by ASEC, the senior technical committee authorized to issue criteria without further AICPA Council clearance. ASEC follows due process, including public exposure, before finalizing criteria.

Example

Why a customer can rely on the benchmark

A hospital system considering Northwind Payroll as a vendor asks for Northwind's SOC 2 report. The hospital's vendor risk reviewer has never met Northwind's auditor and has no way to inspect the audit work directly. The reviewer can still rely on the benchmark the report uses, for three reasons:

  1. The auditor evaluated Northwind against the TSC, a published set of criteria that every report reader can obtain.
  2. ASEC issued the TSC after exposing it for public comment, and ASEC has concluded that the criteria are suitable under the attestation standards.
  3. Other vendors that provide SOC 2 reports to the hospital were evaluated against the same criteria.

Had Northwind's auditor devised its own criteria, the reviewer would first have to judge whether those criteria were relevant, objective, measurable, and complete before the report could mean anything.

The four attributes of "suitable criteria"

Under the attestation standards governing SOC engagements, criteria must meet all four:

R

Relevance

Criteria are relevant to the system being evaluated

O

Objectivity

Criteria are free from bias

M

Measurability

Criteria permit reasonably consistent measurement

C

Completeness

Criteria do not omit relevant factors that would affect users' decisions

Practice Note The AICPA has formally designated the TSC as suitable criteria. For this reason, service auditors use the TSC as the benchmark and do not develop criteria of their own.
Standard History

The 2017 Criteria and 2022 Revisions

2017
TSC Issued The original criteria were published, aligned to the COSO 2013 framework and organized into five categories.
2022
Points of Focus Revised The points of focus were updated to address evolving threats, new privacy laws, data management practices, and the distinction between controllers and processors.
Now
Current Standard Designated "2017 TSC with Revised Points of Focus (2022)." The criteria are unchanged from 2017.
Note The criteria did not change in 2022; only the points of focus were revised. Existing control narratives therefore do not need to be re-mapped to new criteria. The 2022 revisions describe additional ways of meeting the same outcomes.

1.3

Criteria vs. points of focus

In plain terms

Each criterion in the TSC states an outcome. Beneath each criterion, the TSC lists points of focus, which describe characteristics often present when the outcome is achieved. Points of focus help management and the auditor think through a criterion, and TSP 100 states that using the criteria does not require an assessment of whether each point of focus is addressed. GRC staff who treat points of focus as a checklist can spend effort on items that do not fit their organization and can misread what an auditor is asking.

Key terms
Point of focus

An important characteristic of a criterion. Points of focus may help management and the practitioner evaluate whether controls were suitably designed and operated effectively to achieve the entity's objectives based on the criteria (TSP 100, para. .04).

Trust services categories

The five groupings into which the criteria are classified: security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, and privacy. An engagement may address one category or several in combination.

Supplemental criteria

Criteria that the TSC adds beyond the 17 COSO principles, addressing logical and physical access, system operations, change management, and risk mitigation. In the TSC document, supplemental content appears in italics.

Common Misconception

The distinction between criteria and points of focus is frequently misunderstood. An example from performance evaluation illustrates it. A criterion for a manager might be that the manager develops team members; this is the outcome. Points of focus might include holding regular one-on-one meetings, giving constructive feedback, and providing opportunities for growth. None of these practices is required, since a manager may develop a team by other means, but each is a useful characteristic to consider. The TSC is organized on the same principle.

Criteria = the outcomes that must be achieved.

Points of focus = important characteristics that may help management and the practitioner evaluate whether a criterion is met.

Example

Reading the points of focus under CC6.4

Northwind Payroll's staff work from a single leased office. A GRC analyst preparing for the SOC 2 examination reads CC6.4, which requires the entity to restrict physical access to facilities and protected information assets to authorized personnel. The analyst then compares the four points of focus listed beneath the criterion with current practice:

  1. Creates or modifies physical access: office badges are issued only after a manager approves the request.
  2. Removes physical access: badges are deactivated on an employee's last day.
  3. Recovers physical devices: laptops and badges are collected when an employee leaves.
  4. Reviews physical access: Northwind performs no periodic review.

The absence of a review does not by itself mean that CC6.4 is unmet, since points of focus are aids to evaluation. The analyst considers whether the outcome is achieved without one and concludes that a quarterly comparison of active badges against the current staff list is a reasonable addition for an office of this size.

Requirement Use of the TSC does not require an assessment of every point of focus. Some points of focus may not apply to a given organization, and this is acceptable. Treating points of focus as a mandatory checklist is a common error.
Practice · Classification

Criterion or point of focus?

Drag each statement into the category it belongs to, or select a statement and then a category. When every statement is placed, check your sorting.

"The entity restricts physical access to facilities to authorized personnel."
"Recovers entity devices when an employee no longer requires access."
"System processing is complete, valid, accurate, timely, and authorized."
"Conducts vulnerability scans on a periodic basis."
"The entity authorizes, modifies, or removes access based on roles."
"Reviews access roles and rules on a periodic basis."
Criterion

The required outcome

Point of focus

A supporting characteristic

Criteria typically describe a high-level outcome the entity must achieve. Points of focus describe specific practices that could serve as evidence that the outcome is being met. They are not the only valid evidence, and not all of them apply to every organization.

How to read the TSC document

Three formatting conventions indicate the source and applicability of each criterion and point of focus:

Regular font
Derived directly from the COSO Internal Control framework. These foundational concepts will be familiar to financial auditors.
Italics
Supplemental content added specifically for the trust services criteria, with guidance tailored to security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, and privacy.
Bold italics
Applies only at the system level (for example, in SOC 2). Indicates whether the guidance applies to a given engagement type.
Checkpoint · Highlight

Reviewing an analyst's note on CC6.4

A Northwind Payroll analyst wrote this note after comparing office practice with the points of focus under CC6.4. Select the sentences that read the criterion and its points of focus correctly. Select a sentence again to clear it.

CC6.4 states the outcome we must achieve: physical access to our facilities and protected information assets is restricted to authorized personnel. All four points of focus must be in place before the auditor can conclude that CC6.4 is met. We do not perform a periodic review of badge access. For that reason, CC6.4 has failed. The question is whether access is still restricted to authorized personnel without a periodic review. The points of focus are the only evidence the auditor will accept for this criterion.

1.4

Where the TSC is used

In plain terms

The TSC is a set of criteria, and several different kinds of engagement use it. An engagement is the defined piece of work that a CPA firm agrees to perform for a client. Some engagements end in an opinion, a formal conclusion signed by the CPA; others end only in findings and recommendations. The type of engagement determines what report is produced, who may read it, and what the CPA concludes, so GRC staff need to know which engagement their organization is undergoing.

Key terms
Attestation engagement

An engagement in which a CPA performs work under the AICPA Statements on Standards for Attestation Engagements (SSAEs). Examination engagements and agreed-upon procedures engagements are both attestation engagements.

Opinion

The conclusion a practitioner expresses in an examination engagement about subject matter, or an assertion about it, in relation to a set of criteria. Agreed-upon procedures and consulting engagements do not produce an opinion.

Service organization

An organization that provides services to customers, where the controls over those services matter to the customers. A SOC 2 examination reports on the controls of a service organization over a system.

Type 1 and Type 2

The two forms of SOC 2 report. A Type 1 report addresses the design of controls at a point in time. A Type 2 report covers a specified period and adds an opinion on operating effectiveness, along with a detailed description of the tests performed and their results.

Scope of Use

The TSC is used in several engagement types. For GRC staff at a service organization, SOC 2 is likely to be the most frequent. Familiarity with the full range of engagements is nonetheless useful, because the engagement type shapes how the criteria are interpreted and applied.

Source text · TSP 100, para. .25

The governing standards precede the engagement types. Under paragraph .25, each of these engagements is an attestation engagement performed under the AICPA's Statements on Standards for Attestation Engagements (SSAEs). The relevant standards are AT-C 105 (concepts common to all attestation engagements, including independence, suitable criteria, and the practitioner's responsibilities), AT-C 205 (assertion-based examination engagements, the form most SOC 2 engagements take), and AT-C 215 (agreed-upon procedures engagements). The CPA performing the work is called a practitioner in the TSC document and a service auditor in the AICPA SOC 2 Guide; both terms refer to the same role. Footnote 9 adds a limitation: practitioners may not perform a review engagement of internal control under the attestation standards, so only examination and agreed-upon procedures (AUP) engagements are available.

Example

One company, several engagements over time

Northwind Payroll has never been audited. A large prospective customer asks for a SOC 2 Type 2 report before it will sign a contract. Northwind might proceed as follows:

  1. It engages a practitioner for readiness work. The practitioner compares Northwind's controls with the TSC and reports gaps and recommendations, with no opinion.
  2. After closing the gaps, Northwind undergoes a SOC 2 Type 1 examination, which reports on the design of its controls at a single point in time.
  3. It then undergoes a Type 2 examination covering the following six months, which adds an opinion on whether the controls operated effectively throughout that period.
  4. Because a SOC 2 report is restricted in use, Northwind also obtains a SOC 3 report, a general-use summary it can post on its website.

The TSC serves as the benchmark at every step. Each engagement differs in the conclusion it produces and in who may read the result.

Select any engagement type below for further detail.

SOC 2
SOC 2 (Type 1 / Type 2)
Report on controls at a service organization, restricted use
Examines a service organization's controls relevant to one or more trust services categories. Type 1 reports on suitability of design at a point in time. Type 2 covers a period (typically 6 or 12 months) and includes operating effectiveness; it is the report most enterprise customers request during vendor due diligence.
Expand →
SOC 3
SOC 3 Engagement
General-use summary report
Addresses subject matter similar to SOC 2 and produces a general-use report. The report includes the practitioner's opinion and omits detailed test results. It is often published on websites and marketing pages as a public-facing summary, since a full SOC 2 report would be too sensitive to share openly.
Expand →
SOC
Cyber
SOC for Cybersecurity
Entity-wide cybersecurity program review
Examines an entity's cybersecurity risk management program, which is typically broader in scope than a single system. The TSC serves as the control criteria. The engagement is commonly selected by organizations seeking to demonstrate cybersecurity maturity at the entity level.
Expand →
SOC
Supply
SOC for Supply Chain
Engagement for producers, manufacturers, and distributors
Intended for entities that produce, manufacture, or distribute products, and applies the TSC to the systems supporting those activities. It is less common than SOC 2, although adoption is increasing, particularly where supply chain transparency and risk management are concerns.
Expand →
Ready
Readiness / Consulting
Pre-audit gap assessment
Pre-audit work that evaluates an organization's current position against the TSC. This work is performed under consulting standards. The practitioner provides findings and recommendations and expresses no opinion. Readiness work is a common starting point for organizations new to SOC 2.
Expand →
Activity · Scenario Matching

Select the appropriate engagement type for each of five scenarios

Each scenario describes an organization's assurance need. Select the engagement type that addresses it.

Scenario 1
"An enterprise prospect requires assurance that the organization's controls operated effectively over a six-month period, and has asked for detailed test results in addition to an opinion on design."
SOC 2 Type 2. Type 2 covers a period (typically 6 or 12 months) and includes detailed tests of operating effectiveness. Type 1 addresses design only, at a point in time.
Scenario 2
"The marketing team requires a general-use summary report that can be published on the company website without a nondisclosure agreement. The report should show that the organization has been audited without disclosing detailed test results."
SOC 3. SOC 3 is the general-use summary report. It covers the same subject matter as SOC 2 and contains the practitioner's opinion without detailed test results.
Scenario 3
"The board requires entity-wide cybersecurity assurance that covers the organization's entire cybersecurity risk management program and is independent of any specific service or system."
SOC for Cybersecurity. This examines the entity's cybersecurity risk management program at the entity level, which is broader than a single system or service.
Scenario 4
"A manufacturing partner requires assurance about the organization's production and distribution controls, including the controls over how products are made and shipped as well as IT controls."
SOC for Supply Chain. Designed for entities producing, manufacturing, or distributing products. Applies the TSC to systems supporting those activities.
Scenario 5
"The organization has never undergone a SOC 2 examination. Before committing to a formal audit, leadership wants to identify existing gaps and has requested findings and recommendations without an opinion."
Readiness / Consulting. Pre-audit work is performed under consulting standards (CS section 100) and is not an attestation engagement. The practitioner provides findings and recommendations and expresses no opinion (TSP 100, para. .28).

1.5

Same criterion, different lens

In plain terms

Many criteria end with the phrase "to meet the entity's objectives." The words stay the same in every engagement, while the objectives they refer to depend on the engagement type. In a SOC 2 examination, the objectives are the commitments the service organization has made to its customers and the system requirements that follow from them. In a SOC for Cybersecurity examination, they are the cybersecurity objectives of the entity. GRC staff who know which frame applies can answer a question about a criterion with the evidence that frame calls for.

Key terms
Entity's objectives

The goals that controls are meant to support. Because the effectiveness of controls cannot be separated from the objectives they serve, many criteria include the phrase "to meet the entity's objectives," and its interpretation depends on the engagement (TSP 100, para. .18).

Cybersecurity risk management program

The subject of a SOC for Cybersecurity examination: the processes and controls an entity uses to manage cybersecurity risk. Depending on scope, it may cover the entire entity, a subsidiary or division, a function, or a particular type of information (TSP 100, para. .24).

Engagement Type and Interpretation

Many TSC criteria contain the phrase "to meet the entity's objectives." The criterion text is fixed, but the interpretation of that phrase depends on the type of engagement. The same criterion can therefore carry different meanings in a SOC 2 examination and in a SOC for Cybersecurity examination.

CC6.4 provides a worked example. The criterion reads:

"The entity restricts physical access to facilities and protected information assets (for example, data center facilities, backup media storage, and other sensitive locations) to authorized personnel to meet the entity's objectives."

The wording is identical across engagement types, although the meaning of "to meet the entity's objectives" changes:

In a SOC 2 engagement

"to meet the entity's objectives" means to meet the service organization's commitments and system requirements. Service commitments are declarations made to customers (often in MSAs, SLAs, or privacy notices). System requirements are how the system must function to achieve those commitments. CC6.4 is applied only to controls within the trust services categories included in the SOC 2 scope.

In a SOC for Cybersecurity exam

"to meet the entity's objectives" means to meet the entity's cybersecurity objectives. Cybersecurity objectives address the cybersecurity risks that could affect the entity's compliance, reporting, and operational objectives. CC6.4 is applied across the entity's cybersecurity risk management program, which is broader in scope than a single system.

Practice Note When a customer or auditor asks how the entity meets CC6.4, the appropriate answer depends on the engagement. In a SOC 2 examination, GRC staff would identify the relevant service commitments and explain how the physical access controls support them. In a SOC for Cybersecurity examination, they would refer to the entity-wide cybersecurity objectives.

Two terms to know

These two terms recur throughout SOC 2 work, and GRC staff should be familiar with both.

Service commitments

Declarations made by management to customers regarding the performance of one or more of the entity's systems. Communicated through written contracts, service-level agreements, or public statements such as a privacy notice. Baseline commitments apply to all customers; specific commitments are negotiated with individual customers.

System requirements

How the system must function to achieve the entity's commitments to customers, relevant laws and regulations, industry guidelines, or other business objectives. System requirements are the internal obligations that follow from the external commitments.

Activity · Identification

Identify the engagement frame from the auditor's question

Auditors phrase questions about the same criterion differently depending on the engagement type. Read each question and select the frame being applied.

How do your physical access controls support meeting your 99.9% uptime SLA commitment to customers?
SOC 2. The reference to a commitment to customers, and specifically to an SLA, reflects the SOC 2 interpretation of "to meet the entity's objectives" as meeting service commitments (TSP 100, para. .19).
How does this control map to your enterprise-wide cybersecurity risk management program objectives?
SOC for Cybersecurity. The phrase "enterprise-wide cybersecurity risk management program" indicates the SOC for Cybersecurity frame, under which the criterion is applied across the entity as a whole instead of within a specific service organization system (TSP 100, paras. .23–.24).
Walk me through how this physical access control supports your product manufacturing and distribution objectives.
SOC for Supply Chain. The reference to manufacturing and distribution objectives indicates the supply chain frame, in which the engagement examines controls over production, manufacturing, and distribution systems.
For our pre-audit walkthrough, what gaps did you identify against CC6.4? What is the remediation timeline before the formal audit?
Readiness. The terms "pre-audit," "gaps," and "remediation timeline before the formal audit" indicate a readiness or consulting engagement. Such an engagement identifies gaps under CS section 100 and, unlike an attestation engagement, does not result in an opinion.

Module 2

The Five Trust Services Categories

This module defines each of the five categories, distinguishes those that are frequently confused, and explains when each belongs in the scope of an engagement.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this module
  • Define each of the five trust services categories
  • Distinguish categories that are commonly confused, particularly confidentiality and privacy
  • Identify when each category should be in scope for an engagement
  • Explain why Security uses only Common Criteria while other categories add specific criteria
Module 2 · Begin
2.0

The five categories at a glance

In plain terms

The Trust Services Criteria (TSC) sort their requirements into five categories. Each category names one quality a system is expected to have: security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, or privacy. The categories a SOC 2 report addresses are chosen when the engagement is scoped, and security is the base on which the others rest. A GRC professional needs this structure to read a SOC 2 report and to help decide what an engagement will cover.

Key terms
Trust services category

One of the five groupings of criteria in TSP 100: security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, and privacy. A practitioner may report on any category individually or in combination with others (TSP 100, para. .11).

Common criteria

Criteria shared by all five categories, identified by the prefix CC. For security, the common criteria are the complete set, and no additional control activity criteria are needed (TSP 100, para. .10).

Category-specific criteria

Additional criteria that apply to one category only: the A series for availability, PI for processing integrity, C for confidentiality, and P for privacy. A complete set for any of these categories is the common criteria plus that category's series.

Context

The TSC defines five categories, and they do not carry equal weight. Security forms the foundation and is included in nearly every engagement. The remaining four (availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, and privacy) build on that foundation, each addressing a specific aspect of how systems and information are expected to perform.

Example

Choosing categories at Northwind Payroll

Northwind Payroll is a fictional SaaS company that calculates and pays wages on behalf of client businesses. Its clients have asked for a SOC 2 report, and the scoping discussion proceeds as follows.

  1. Every client expects the payroll system to be protected against unauthorized access, so security is included. The common criteria are evaluated.
  2. Clients depend on payroll running on the scheduled date, so availability is added. The A series is evaluated together with the common criteria.
  3. Clients rely on the accuracy of the pay calculations, so processing integrity is considered for the payroll system, which brings in the PI series.
  4. The common criteria apply across all three selected categories, and each added category contributes its own series on top of them.
The Hierarchy

Security as the foundation for four additional categories

Privacy
Personal information lifecycle
Confidentiality
Designated sensitive information
Processing Integrity
Complete, valid, accurate, timely, authorized
Availability
Accessible for operation and use
Security
The foundation · almost always in scope
Principle Security is the foundation of the framework. An entity that cannot protect its systems and information from unauthorized access cannot achieve its availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, or privacy objectives.

The complete set for availability

2.1

Security

In plain terms

Security asks whether information and systems are protected against unauthorized access, unauthorized disclosure, and damage. It covers information at each stage (collection or creation, use, processing, transmission, and storage) as well as the systems that handle it. A failure of security can undermine every other category, so security controls make up most of a typical SOC 2 control set. A GRC professional will spend much of any SOC 2 effort on this category.

Key terms
Unauthorized access

Entry into, or use of, information or systems by a person or process without permission. Protection against it is the first concern named in the definition of the security category.

Segregation of duties

Dividing tasks so that no single person can both carry out and conceal an error or improper action, for example by requiring that a change be approved by someone other than its author. TSP 100 lists the breakdown or circumvention of segregation of duties among the events security controls prevent or detect.

Control matrix

A working document, usually a spreadsheet, that maps each applicable criterion to the controls the entity operates to meet it. It organizes both the preparation for and the testing of a SOC 2 examination.

Security
Information and systems are protected against unauthorized access, unauthorized disclosure, and damage that could compromise availability, integrity, confidentiality, or privacy.
What security covers: Information during collection or creation, use, processing, transmission, and storage, together with the systems that use, process, transmit, or store information.
What security controls prevent or detect: Breakdown of segregation of duties, system failure, incorrect processing, theft or unauthorized removal of information, misuse of software, and improper access to or use of information.
Common Criteria only No category-specific criteria Almost always in scope
Example

Tracing one security control at Northwind Payroll

A Northwind Payroll engineer leaves the company. Under the access management procedure, the engineer's accounts are disabled on the last day of employment.

  1. The control supports security directly: a former employee who kept access could view or alter payroll data without authorization.
  2. The same unauthorized access could also disrupt a payroll run (an availability concern) or expose client salary files (a confidentiality concern).
  3. Logical access criteria are common criteria, which apply to all five categories (TSP 100, para. .09). In the control matrix, this single control therefore supports every category in scope.
Practice note Security accounts for most of a SOC 2 control matrix, including access management, change management, system operations, and incident response. The other categories add specific requirements to this base.
Practice · Highlight

Finding the security events in a risk review

Read this excerpt from Northwind Payroll's quarterly risk review. Select the phrases that describe events security controls are meant to prevent or detect. Select a phrase again to clear it.

The review team noted several concerns for the quarter. One engineer is able to approve and deploy code changes without a second reviewer. A laptop lost in transit could permit the removal of client payroll files. An audit of accounts found that a former contractor could still sign in to the payroll database. Separately, several clients asked for a new dashboard layout with additional charts, and the sales team proposed a change to the prices listed on the public website.

Checkpoint

Which statement best describes how security relates to the other four categories?

2.2

Availability

In plain terms

Availability asks whether information and systems are accessible for operation and use when the entity needs them to meet its objectives. The category evaluates controls that support that accessibility, such as capacity monitoring, environmental protection, data backup, and recovery testing. The criteria set no uptime percentage. Any specific target comes from the commitments the entity has made to its customers, and a GRC professional needs this distinction to explain accurately what a SOC 2 report says about uptime.

Key terms
Service commitments

Declarations made by management to customers regarding the performance of one or more of the entity's systems. They generally appear in written contracts, service-level agreements, or public statements (TSP 100, para. .19).

Service level agreement (SLA)

A contract term that states a measurable level of service, such as a percentage of monthly uptime. An SLA is one common source of service commitments.

Functionality

The specific functions a system performs. The availability category does not address it (TSP 100, para. .12).

Usability

The ability of users to apply system functions to the performance of specific tasks or problems. It also lies outside the availability category.

Common misconception

Availability is among the most frequently misunderstood categories. It is often equated with uptime, such as a 99.9% service level agreement (SLA). In TSC terms, availability concerns whether the entity has controls that support the accessibility of the system when needed. The category does not establish a specific performance target.

Availability
Information and systems are available for operation and use to meet the entity's objectives.
What availability includes: The accessibility of information used by the entity's systems; the accessibility of products or services provided to customers; controls supporting operation, monitoring, and maintenance.
What availability excludes: A minimum acceptable performance level (the TSC does not set one); system functionality (what the system does); and usability (how effectively users apply system functions to specific tasks).
A1.1 Capacity A1.2 Environmental + Backup A1.3 Recovery testing
Example

Reading an uptime commitment at Northwind Payroll

Northwind Payroll's client contracts promise 99.9% monthly uptime. A client asks whether the SOC 2 report confirms that figure.

  1. The 99.9% figure is a service commitment stated in the contract. The TSC did not set it.
  2. The availability criteria ask whether Northwind has controls that support meeting the commitment: monitoring processing capacity (A1.1), maintaining environmental protections, data backup processes, and recovery infrastructure (A1.2), and testing recovery plan procedures (A1.3).
  3. The examination therefore evaluates those controls against the criteria. The answer to the client is that the report addresses the controls supporting the 99.9% commitment.
Activity · True or false

Availability: true or false

Select each statement to reveal whether it is true or false in TSC terms.

Availability requires a minimum 99.9% uptime SLA.
False. The TSC does not set a minimum performance level. A specific uptime commitment forms part of the entity's service commitments and is separate from the criteria.
Availability addresses controls for capacity, environmental protection, and recovery testing.
True. These are the three category-specific availability criteria: A1.1, A1.2, and A1.3.
Availability evaluates whether the system offers appropriate features for users.
False. Features relate to functionality, which the availability category explicitly excludes. Availability concerns accessibility; what the system does lies outside its scope.
Availability and security overlap, because a compromised system cannot be considered available.
True. This overlap is one reason Security serves as the foundation. Many security controls, such as incident response and boundary protection, directly support availability outcomes.
Checkpoint · Highlight

What a client can learn about availability

A client sends Northwind Payroll this request about its SOC 2 report. Select the questions that the availability criteria address. Select a phrase again to clear it.

Before renewing our contract, we would like to know whether you monitor processing capacity as payroll volumes grow, whether your recovery plan procedures are tested, whether the new reporting module offers the export formats we asked for, and whether the TSC requires you to guarantee 99.9% uptime.

2.3

Processing Integrity

In plain terms

Processing integrity asks whether a system does its job correctly, meaning that its processing is complete, valid, accurate, timely, and authorized. It matters most for systems whose results customers rely on, such as billing, order management, or manufacturing systems. An entity may run many systems, so this category is usually applied to specific ones. A GRC professional must judge whether a system's outputs matter enough to customers to place processing integrity in scope.

Key terms
Inputs and outputs

Inputs are the data a system receives for processing; outputs are the results it produces, such as invoices or reports. The PI series treats inputs (PI1.2), processing (PI1.3), outputs (PI1.4), and storage (PI1.5) as separate stages.

Valid and authorized

Valid processing handles only genuine transactions that meet the system's specifications. Authorized processing takes place only with approval from someone permitted to give it.

System or functional level

Applying a category to a particular system or business function, such as billing, instead of to every system the entity operates. Processing integrity is usually scoped this way (TSP 100, para. .12).

Applicability

Processing integrity addresses whether a system performs its intended functions accurately and on time. The category is most relevant to systems that process transactions, manufacture products, or produce outputs on which customers depend. It appears in SOC 2 reports less often than security or availability; where it is relevant, however, it is central to the engagement.

Processing Integrity
System processing is complete, valid, accurate, timely, and authorized to meet the entity's objectives.
The five attributes: These attributes define the outcomes that processing integrity controls must support.
C
Complete
V
Valid
A
Accurate
T
Timely
A
Authorized
Scoping note: Processing integrity is usually addressed at the system or functional level rather than entity-wide. An entity may operate many systems, and PI is typically applied to specific ones, such as a billing system, an order management system, or, in a supply chain context, a manufacturing system.
PI1.1 Information specs PI1.2 Inputs PI1.3 Processing PI1.4 Outputs PI1.5 Storage
Example

Applying the five attributes to a payroll run

Northwind Payroll includes processing integrity for its payroll calculation system, the system its clients rely on most. A single pay run shows how each attribute applies.

  1. Complete: every employee on the client's roster is paid, with none skipped or paid twice.
  2. Valid: payments go only to employees who exist and are active on the roster.
  3. Accurate: gross pay, deductions, and net pay are calculated correctly.
  4. Timely: payments are issued by the scheduled pay date.
  5. Authorized: the run is released only after the client's designated approver signs off.

Northwind's marketing website is left out of this scope, because no customer depends on its processing.

Practice · Classification

Inputs, processing, or outputs?

Each statement describes a control over Northwind Payroll's pay run. Drag each control into the stage of processing it addresses, or select a control and then a stage.

Timesheet files uploaded by clients are checked against the required format before they are accepted.
A record is kept of every file a client submits for a pay run.
Calculation errors flagged during the run are corrected before payments are released.

2.4

Confidentiality

In plain terms

Confidentiality asks whether information designated as confidential is protected throughout its life, from collection or creation until its final disposition and removal from the entity's control. Information receives that designation when a law, regulation, contract, or business decision requires its access, use, retention, and disclosure to be limited. Sensitivity alone does not make information confidential in TSC terms. A GRC professional therefore starts by locating those obligations, since they determine which information the category covers.

Key terms
Confidential information

Information whose custodian is required to limit its access, use, and retention and to restrict its disclosure to defined parties. The requirement may arise from laws, regulations, contracts, or internal business decisions (TSP 100, para. .12).

Custodian

The party that holds or stores information, such as a SaaS provider storing client files. The custodian carries the obligation to protect information designated as confidential.

System boundaries

The specific infrastructure, software, people, procedures, and data necessary to perform a function or provide a service. Confidentiality can restrict disclosure even among parties who otherwise have authorized access within these boundaries.

Disposal

The phase of the data life cycle concerning how an entity removes or destroys data or information. Criterion C1.2 addresses the disposal of confidential information.

Definition of confidential information

Confidentiality concerns the protection of information that has been designated as confidential. Sensitive information is not necessarily confidential in TSC terms. Information becomes confidential when a contractual, legal, regulatory, or business obligation exists to limit its access, use, retention, and disclosure.

Confidentiality
Information designated as confidential is protected to meet the entity's objectives.
What confidentiality addresses: Protecting designated information from collection or creation through final disposition; limiting its access, use, and retention; and restricting its disclosure to defined parties, including parties that may otherwise have authorized access within the system boundaries.
Where confidentiality requirements come from: Laws or regulations · Contracts or customer agreements · Internal designations (e.g., proprietary information for entity personnel only).
C1.1 Identify + maintain C1.2 Disposal
Example

Deciding what Northwind Payroll must treat as confidential

Northwind Payroll's master services agreement (MSA) with each client limits access to client salary data to a named support team and requires deletion of that data within 90 days after the contract ends.

  1. The MSA creates an obligation to limit access and disclosure, so the salary data is confidential information.
  2. Under C1.1, Northwind identifies the data and maintains it under those restrictions. Other engineers can reach the database within the system boundaries, yet the MSA confines access to the named team, so their access is removed.
  3. Under C1.2, Northwind disposes of a departing client's data within the agreed 90 days.
  4. Northwind's published pricing page carries no restriction from any source, so it falls outside the category.

2.5

Privacy

In plain terms

Privacy asks whether personal information is collected, used, retained, disclosed, and disposed of in a way that meets the entity's objectives. It applies only to information about identifiable individuals and follows that information through its whole lifecycle. The individuals themselves figure in the criteria, which address notice to them, their choices and consent, and their access to their own information. A GRC professional needs to establish early whether personal information is in the system and what role the entity plays in handling it.

Key terms
Personal information

Information that is about, or can be related to, an identifiable individual (TSP 100, glossary). Names, home addresses, and tax identification numbers are common examples.

Data subject

The individual about whom personal information is collected, such as an employee whose wages a payroll system processes.

Data controller

An organization that, alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes for and the means by which personal data is processed.

Data processor

An organization that processes personal data at the direction of a data controller. Many service organizations act in this role for their business-to-business (B2B) customers.

Scope and complexity

Privacy is the most complex category, with eight sub-areas and the largest set of additional criteria. Its scope is also specific: privacy applies only to personal information. A B2B service organization that does not interact directly with end users may not need to include privacy in scope. When privacy is in scope, it requires substantial attention.

Privacy
Personal information is collected, used, retained, disclosed, and disposed of to meet the entity's objectives.
Scope distinction: Privacy applies only to personal information, whereas confidentiality applies to many types of sensitive information. Personal information can be both confidential and subject to the privacy criteria. Other confidential information, such as trade secrets, is not subject to the privacy criteria.
18 criteria total 8 sub-areas Largest category
Example

Is privacy relevant at Northwind Payroll?

Before deciding whether to include privacy, Northwind Payroll examines the data in its system and its relationship to the people that data describes.

  1. Northwind's system stores the names, bank account numbers, and tax identifiers of each client's employees. Each item relates to an identifiable person, so it is personal information, and privacy is a candidate for scope.
  2. The client businesses decide which employee data is collected and for what purpose; Northwind processes it on their instructions. The clients are therefore the data controllers and Northwind is a data processor.
  3. Because Northwind does not collect the data directly from the employees, a criterion such as P3.1 on collection may be inapplicable to its system (TSP 100, para. .11).
  4. The same salary records are restricted by the MSA, so they fall under confidentiality as well as privacy.
Practice · Highlight

Finding the personal information in a system description

Read this excerpt from the description of Northwind Payroll's system. Select the items that are personal information. Select a phrase again to clear it.

For each client business, the payroll system stores the names of the client's employees, each employee's bank account number, and each employee's tax identification number. It also stores the client company's published business address, the tax rate tables used in pay calculations, and the schedule of pay dates agreed with each client.

The eight privacy sub-areas

Privacy criteria are organized into eight thematic groups, each addressing a different aspect of how personal information is handled across its lifecycle.

P1
Notice & Communication
Provides notice to data subjects about privacy practices
P2
Choice & Consent
Communicates choices and obtains consent
P3
Collection
Collects personal information consistent with privacy objectives
P4
Use, Retention, Disposal
Limits use, retention, and disposal appropriately
P5
Access
Provides data subjects access for review and correction
P6
Disclosure & Notification
Discloses appropriately, notifies of breaches
P7
Quality
Maintains accurate, up-to-date, complete, relevant data
P8
Monitoring & Enforcement
Addresses inquiries, complaints, disputes; monitors compliance

Data Controller vs. Data Processor

The 2022 revisions added markers to the privacy points of focus to help distinguish which apply where:

Data Controller
[C]Determines the purposes and means of processing personal data. Has the direct relationship with data subjects.
Data Processor
[P]Processes personal data on behalf of a controller. Many B2B SaaS providers fall here.
Practice note A SaaS provider that processes personal data on behalf of B2B customers is typically a data processor, and its customers are the controllers. Some privacy points of focus, such as providing notice to data subjects, will not apply to the provider because it has no direct relationship with those data subjects.

2.6

Frequently confused categories

In plain terms

This lesson brings together the distinctions that most often cause errors in scoping an engagement or reading a report. The most common confusion is between confidentiality and privacy, which overlap when information is both personal and designated as confidential. Three further distinctions concern availability and uptime, the reason security relies on the common criteria alone, and the uncommon engagement that leaves security out. A GRC professional who can state these distinctions clearly can answer most customer questions about what a SOC 2 report covers.

Confidentiality and privacy compared

Aspect
Confidentiality
Privacy
Scope
Any sensitive information
Only personal information
Source of obligation
Contracts, laws, business needs
Privacy laws, consent, fair information principles
Subject involvement
None directly
Data subjects have rights (access, correction, deletion)
Lifecycle focus
Protection from disclosure
Full lifecycle management
Illustrative cases Customer financial data may be both confidential and subject to the privacy criteria. A trade secret is confidential and falls outside the privacy criteria. A publicly available email address is not confidential, although it may be subject to the privacy criteria depending on how it was collected and used.
Example

Sorting a client's questions at Northwind Payroll

A Northwind Payroll client asks which categories in the SOC 2 report cover four items. The GRC analyst works through each one.

  1. Employee salary records: personal information, and restricted by the MSA. Both privacy and confidentiality apply.
  2. Source code for Northwind's tax calculation engine: designated confidential by an internal business decision, and it contains no personal information. Confidentiality applies; privacy does not.
  3. The client's published business address: no restriction applies, and it identifies a company instead of an individual. Neither category applies.
  4. The 99.9% uptime promise: a service commitment. The availability criteria evaluate the controls that support meeting it.

Additional distinctions

Activity · Review

Three further category misunderstandings

A
Availability vs. uptime/performance
▼

The availability category concerns controls that support accessibility, whereas an uptime SLA is a service commitment. The two are related but distinct: the SLA states what the entity has committed to, and the availability criteria evaluate whether the entity's controls support meeting its commitments.

B
Why Security uses only Common Criteria
▼

ASEC determined that the Common Criteria fully cover the security category, so no additional control activity criteria are required for security. Each of the other categories adds its own specific criteria to the Common Criteria. For this reason, most SOC 2 reports include security together with selected other categories.

C
When Security might not be in scope
▼

This situation is uncommon but possible. If a SOC 2 examination addresses only availability (or another single non-security category), the relevant subset of access, operations, and change management criteria still applies; those criteria are evaluated only for their effect on the selected category.

Checkpoint

A company compiles a marketing list from email addresses that individuals have listed publicly. Which category may apply to that list?

Module 3

How the Criteria Are Organized

The TSC follows a defined structure. An understanding of how the Common Criteria align to COSO, where the supplemental criteria fit, and how the document's formatting conventions work makes the standard considerably easier to use.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this module
  • Describe the complete structure of the TSC
  • Explain how the Common Criteria align with COSO
  • Identify which criteria series applies to which subject area
  • Read the TSC document conventions correctly (font styles and [C]/[P] markers)
Module 3 · Begin
3.1

Common Criteria & the COSO alignment

In plain terms

The trust services criteria were built on an older and widely used model of internal control called COSO. The first five groups of Common Criteria, CC1 through CC5, follow the five parts of that model, and each criterion in those groups matches one COSO principle. A GRC professional who knows this alignment can explain SOC 2 requirements in terms that auditors, executives, and board members already use for financial controls.

Key terms
COSO

The Committee of Sponsoring Organizations of the Treadway Commission, a joint initiative of five private-sector organizations that publishes frameworks on internal control, enterprise risk management, and fraud deterrence. Its internal control framework, revised in 2013, is the model the Common Criteria follow.

Internal control

A process, carried out by an entity's board, management, and other personnel, designed to provide reasonable assurance that objectives relating to operations, reporting, and compliance are achieved (TSP 100, glossary).

Component and principle

COSO organizes internal control into 5 broad components (such as Control Environment and Risk Assessment). Under those components sit 17 principles, each a more specific statement of what effective internal control requires.

Common Criteria

The criteria shared by all five trust services categories. They apply to every SOC 2 examination, whichever categories are in scope.

Context

The Common Criteria are aligned to COSO, the leading framework for internal control. Through this alignment, the AICPA placed the trust services criteria within the broader internal control discussion already under way among boards, auditors, and senior leadership.

COSO comprises 17 principles organized into 5 components. The Common Criteria series CC1 through CC5 map directly to those 5 components, one series per component, and the individual criteria within each series map to the corresponding COSO principles.

Example

Explaining a SOC 2 criterion to the audit committee

Northwind Payroll, a fictional payroll SaaS company, is preparing for its first SOC 2 examination. A member of the board's audit committee asks how SOC 2 relates to the financial controls the committee already oversees. The GRC analyst answers in three steps.

  1. The analyst points to Northwind's code of conduct and annual ethics attestation, which the financial auditors already review.
  2. The analyst explains that these support COSO Principle 1, a commitment to integrity and ethical values, within the Control Environment component.
  3. The analyst then shows that CC1.1 in the trust services criteria is the same principle. The existing ethics program therefore supports a SOC 2 criterion as well.

The committee member now sees SOC 2 as an extension of a familiar framework, and the analyst has avoided a lengthy introduction to a new standard.

3.2

Supplemental Common Criteria (CC6–CC9)

In plain terms

COSO was written for internal control in general, so it says little about specific technology practices such as granting system access or approving software changes. The trust services criteria fill that gap with four additional series, CC6 through CC9. All four expand a single COSO principle about putting controls into action through policies and procedures. Because these series describe access, operations, change, and vendor practices, they account for much of the daily work of a GRC team.

Key terms
Supplemental criteria

The criteria TSP 100 adds to supplement COSO Principle 12. They are organized as logical and physical access controls, system operations, change management, and risk mitigation (TSP 100, para. .08).

Control activity

An action established through policies and procedures that helps ensure management's directives to mitigate risks to the achievement of objectives are carried out (TSP 100, glossary).

Logical access

Access to information and system components through software, such as user accounts, passwords, and permissions. Physical access refers to entry to facilities and equipment. CC6 addresses both.

Purpose of CC6–CC9

COSO is a general internal control framework that addresses financial reporting, operations, and compliance broadly. Trust services engagements require more specific guidance on technology controls. The TSC therefore adds four supplemental criteria series, CC6 through CC9, all of which fall under COSO Principle 12, "deploys control activities through policies."

Most day-to-day SOC 2 work falls within these four series: access management, system operations, change management, and vendor risk.

Example

Sorting a week of GRC requests

During one week, the GRC analyst at Northwind Payroll receives four requests. Each one falls under a different supplemental series.

  1. Remove system access for an employee who resigned. This concerns how access is provided and removed, so it belongs to CC6, logical and physical access.
  2. Investigate an alert about unusual login activity on a production server. Detecting and responding to anomalies belongs to CC7, system operations.
  3. Confirm that a payroll calculation update was tested and approved before release. Authorizing, testing, and approving changes belongs to CC8, change management.
  4. Review the security report of the cloud hosting provider. Managing risks from vendors and business partners belongs to CC9, risk mitigation.

Sorting requests by series in this way helps the analyst locate the relevant criteria and points of focus quickly.

CC6
Logical & Physical Access
8 criteria · CC6.1–CC6.8
The largest CC series. Identification, authentication, authorization, encryption, physical security, secure disposal, boundary protection, malware defense.
CC7
System Operations
5 criteria · CC7.1–CC7.5
Detection of vulnerabilities and configuration changes, anomaly monitoring, security incident response, and recovery.
CC8
Change Management
1 criterion · CC8.1
A single criterion with extensive points of focus covering the full change lifecycle: identify, authorize, design, test, deploy, and monitor.
CC9
Risk Mitigation
2 criteria · CC9.1–CC9.2
Business continuity, disaster recovery, and third-party / vendor risk management.

Total Common Criteria 17 mapped to COSO (CC1–CC5) + 16 supplemental (CC6–CC9) = 33 Common Criteria. Every category in scope brings all 33 with it. Categories other than Security add specific criteria to that base.
Common misconception

The 33 Common Criteria are shared across every category in scope and are counted once. Adding Availability to a Security-only engagement adds 3 criteria (A1.1–A1.3), for a total of 36. The total is always 33 plus the sum of the category-specific additions. With all five categories in scope, the total is 33 + 3 + 5 + 2 + 18 = 61 criteria; multiplying the Common Criteria by the number of categories (which would yield 165) is incorrect. Leadership and engineering teams raise this scoping error more often than any other, and GRC staff should address it early.

Checkpoint

Northwind Payroll adds a requirement that all production deployments be approved by a second engineer. Which supplemental series does this control most directly address?

3.3

Category-specific criteria

In plain terms

A SOC 2 examination always covers Security, and an entity may choose to add one or more of the other four categories. Each added category brings a small set of its own criteria, which sit on top of the 33 Common Criteria. GRC staff need to calculate the resulting total correctly, because it drives the size of the audit, the evidence requests, and the effort a team should plan for.

Key terms
Trust services category

One of the five subject areas the criteria address: security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, and privacy.

Category-specific criteria

The additional criteria that apply only when their category is in scope, such as A1.1–A1.3 for Availability. Security has none; it is addressed entirely by the Common Criteria.

In scope

Included in the examination. The categories in scope determine which criteria the auditor evaluates.

Category-specific additions

Beyond the Common Criteria, each category other than Security adds its own specific criteria. These criteria address the distinctive features of each category that the Common Criteria do not fully cover.

Use the calculator below to see how the total number of criteria changes according to the categories in scope.

Example

Adding Processing Integrity to the next examination

Northwind Payroll calculates paychecks for its customers, and several customers ask for assurance that those calculations are complete and accurate. Leadership proposes adding Processing Integrity to next year's SOC 2 examination and asks the GRC analyst how much the scope will grow.

  1. The current examination covers Security only, which means the 33 Common Criteria.
  2. Processing Integrity adds 5 category-specific criteria, PI1.1–PI1.5.
  3. The Common Criteria are counted once, so the new total is 33 + 5 = 38.

The analyst reports an increase of 5 criteria. A figure of 71, obtained by counting the 33 Common Criteria a second time for the new category, would overstate the work by a wide margin.

3.4

Reading the TSC document conventions

In plain terms

Each criterion in TSP 100 is followed by a list of points of focus, which describe what meeting the criterion usually looks like. The font of each item tells the reader where it came from and when it applies, and the privacy section adds short bracketed markers for the same purpose. Reading these signals correctly prevents two common errors: treating every point of focus as mandatory, and applying guidance to an engagement it does not cover.

Key terms
Point of focus

An important characteristic of a criterion. Points of focus may assist management and the practitioner in evaluating whether controls were suitably designed and operated effectively. Use of the criteria does not require an assessment of whether each point of focus is addressed (TSP 100, paras. .04 and .07).

System level

An engagement that evaluates a defined system, meaning the infrastructure, software, procedures, and data operated by people to achieve specific business objectives. A SOC 2 examination is performed at the system level.

Data controller

An organization that, alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes for and the means by which personal data is processed (TSP 100, glossary).

Data processor

An organization that processes personal data at the direction of a data controller. A service organization often acts as a processor for its business customers (TSP 100, glossary).

Document conventions

GRC professionals frequently work directly with the TSC document, so its formatting conventions matter. Three font styles indicate the source and applicability of each criterion or point of focus. The privacy section adds two markers that indicate whether content applies to data controllers, data processors, or both.

Source text · TSP 100, paras. .05 and .07

Two paragraphs near the beginning of TSP 100 should inform any reading of the criteria. Paragraph .07: use of the trust services criteria does not require an assessment of whether each point of focus is addressed. Paragraph .05: some points of focus may not be suitable or relevant; management may customize a particular point of focus or substitute other characteristics based on the specific circumstances of the entity. Together, these paragraphs establish that the points of focus (POFs) do not constitute a mandatory checklist, and they call for judgment about which POFs are relevant to the entity's environment. New GRC staff frequently attempt to check off every POF, which creates work the standard does not require. Paragraph .06 further permits the addition of POFs drawn from process or control frameworks to which the entity has committed (for example, NIST or ISO).

Example

Reading a page of the criteria with the conventions in mind

The GRC analyst at Northwind Payroll is drafting control narratives for a SOC 2 examination that includes Privacy. While reading TSP 100, the analyst applies the conventions in order.

  1. Under CC2.2, the analyst finds points of focus in bold italics about communicating system boundaries and system objectives. Because SOC 2 is performed at the system level, these apply to Northwind.
  2. In the privacy section, the analyst considers Northwind's role. Northwind processes employee data at the direction of its employer customers, so it acts mainly as a data processor. Points of focus marked [P] or [P][C] are therefore the likely starting point, such as one marked [P] on responding to data controller requests.
  3. One point of focus describes an activity Northwind does not perform. Under paragraphs .05 and .07, the analyst need not build a control for it and may instead consider other characteristics that fit Northwind's circumstances.

Three formatting conventions

The font style of each criterion or point of focus indicates its source and where it applies.

Regular font
Derived directly from the COSO Internal Control framework. These foundational concepts are familiar to financial auditors.
Italics
Supplemental content added specifically for the trust services criteria, providing tailored guidance for security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, and privacy.
Bold italics
Applies only at the system level (for example, SOC 2). This convention indicates whether the guidance extends to a given engagement type.
Activity · Identification

Identify each formatting convention

Read each example and select the format in which it would appear. Feedback appears after each selection.

"The entity demonstrates a commitment to integrity and ethical values."
A foundational principle that any organization following internal control standards would recognize.
"Identifies threats to system objectives: intentional, unintentional, environmental."
Specific risk concepts that COSO does not address directly and that the TSC adds.
"Communicates the system boundaries, system objectives, and system responsibilities to internal and external users."
Specific guidance that applies only when the engagement is performed at the system level (for example, SOC 2).

Privacy section: [C] and [P] markers

The points of focus in the privacy section include bracketed markers. These markers were added in the 2022 revisions to distinguish applicability to controllers and to processors.

Controller
[C]Likely relevant to a data controller.
Processor
[P]Likely relevant to a data processor.
Both
[P][C]Likely relevant to both roles.

These markers are indicative. Actual applicability depends on the specific facts and circumstances of the entity's operations.

Practice note When reviewing draft auditor work or drafting control narratives, GRC staff should note the font style of each criterion or point of focus. The style indicates whether the item is a foundational COSO concept, TSC-specific guidance, or a requirement that applies only at the system level.
Checkpoint · Highlight

Reviewing a draft team guide

A new team member at Northwind Payroll drafted this guide to the points of focus. Select the phrases that accurately reflect TSP 100. Select a phrase again to clear it.

Points of focus may assist management in evaluating whether controls are suitably designed. For this reason, the team must write a separate control for every point of focus under each criterion in scope. Where a point of focus does not fit Northwind, management may customize it or substitute other characteristics that suit its circumstances. Points of focus in regular font are mandatory because they come from COSO, and points of focus marked [P] must be addressed by every data processor.

Module 4

The Common Criteria in Detail: CC1–CC5

This module turns from the structure of the criteria to their substance. CC1 through CC5 form the COSO-aligned foundation of the Common Criteria: control environment, information and communication, risk assessment, monitoring activities, and control activities.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this module
  • Identify the outcome each of the 17 COSO-aligned criteria requires
  • Recognize where TSC adds technology-specific detail beyond the COSO baseline
  • Map a real business process to multiple Common Criteria
Module 4 · Begin
4.1

The 17 criteria at a glance

In plain terms

The 17 criteria in CC1–CC5 each state a result the entity must achieve, such as holding people accountable for their control responsibilities or identifying changes that could affect internal control. A GRC professional needs a working sense of what each result is and which COSO component it belongs to. With that sense, an auditor's request that cites a criterion number can be turned into a clear question about the entity's own practices.

Key terms
Criteria

The benchmarks used to measure or evaluate the subject matter (TSP 100, glossary). In a SOC 2 examination, each trust services criterion is a benchmark against which the entity's controls are evaluated.

Outcome statement

The wording of a criterion, which describes what the entity achieves (for example, "identifies and analyzes risks") and leaves the choice of specific controls to the entity.

Control

A policy or procedure that is part of the entity's system of internal control. Controls exist to provide reasonable assurance that the entity's principal system objectives are achieved (TSP 100, glossary).

Principle

CC1 through CC5 contain 17 individual criteria distributed across the five COSO components. GRC staff need not memorize the exact wording of each criterion; they should, however, know the outcome each criterion requires and the COSO component to which it belongs.

Each Common Criterion describes an outcome that the entity must achieve. The map below presents all of CC1–CC5, organized by COSO component. Select any criterion to display its outcome statement.

Example

Turning a criterion number into an evidence request

Meridian Health Software, a fictional SaaS company, receives an auditor request for "evidence supporting CC3.4." The GRC analyst does not recall the exact wording and works from structure instead.

  1. CC3 is the Risk Assessment component, so the request concerns how Meridian identifies and evaluates risk.
  2. The outcome of CC3.4 is that the entity identifies and assesses changes that could significantly affect internal control. The TSC additions name changes in systems and technology, vendor relationships, and threats and vulnerabilities.
  3. Meridian moved its hosting to a new cloud provider during the period. The analyst therefore gathers the risk assessment update prepared for that migration and the meeting notes in which management reviewed it.

Knowing the component and the outcome was enough to identify relevant evidence.
