7.2

When a criterion may not apply: the limited circumstances exception

In plain terms

Once a category is in scope, the entity is expected to address every criterion in it. TSP 100 allows one narrow exception: a single criterion may be marked not applicable when it describes an activity the entity simply does not perform. GRC professionals need to know where this line falls, because an N/A designation that cannot be justified will be challenged by the auditor and can weaken the credibility of the whole report.

Key terms
Not applicable (N/A)

A designation that a particular criterion is not relevant to the services the service organization provides and is therefore not applicable to the engagement (TSP 100, para. .11). It applies to individual criteria only.

Data subject

The individual about whom personal information is collected.

Structurally inapplicable

The course’s shorthand for a criterion that describes an activity the entity does not perform at all. A missing or immature control does not make a criterion structurally inapplicable.

Limited-circumstances exception

Once a category is in scope, all of its criteria usually apply. TSP 100 permits a narrow exception. Paragraph .11 states that "in limited circumstances, such as when the scope of the engagement is to report on a system, a particular criterion may not be relevant to the services provided by a service organization and, consequently, is not applicable to the engagement." The paragraph gives an explicit example: P3.1 (collects personal information consistent with privacy objectives) is unlikely to apply to a service organization that does not directly collect personal information from data subjects.

This is one of the few provisions in the TSC that explicitly permits a criterion to be marked N/A, and it is frequently misused. Three conditions must hold before the exception is applied:

1

The category is in scope

An entire category cannot be marked N/A because individual criteria are inconvenient. The exception operates only at the criterion level.

2

The criterion is structurally inapplicable

The criterion describes an activity the entity does not perform. The example in TSP 100 is an entity that does not directly collect personal information from data subjects, for which P3.1 is structurally inapplicable.

3

The justification is documented in the description

The system description must explain why the criterion is not applicable, and auditors will challenge unjustified N/A designations. The absence of controls for a criterion does not establish that the criterion is structurally inapplicable.

Example

Two N/A proposals at Northwind Payroll

A large customer asks Northwind Payroll to add Privacy to its next report, and the GRC lead reviews two proposals from the team.

  1. P3.1 (collection of personal information). Northwind receives employee data from its employer customers and never collects it from employees directly. The category is in scope, the criterion describes an activity Northwind does not perform, and the reason can be stated in the system description. All three conditions hold, so N/A with documented justification is appropriate.
  2. CC9.2 (risks associated with vendors and business partners). The team proposes N/A because Northwind has no formal vendor review program. Northwind does use vendors, including its cloud host, so the activity exists. The second condition fails: the criterion applies, and the missing program is a gap to remediate.
Activity · Applicability judgment

Determining applicability

For each situation, decide whether the criterion applies, may be marked N/A with justification, or does not qualify for the exception. Select the option you would choose.

Situation A. A processor SaaS provider holds customer data on behalf of B2B customers. The customers, rather than the provider, collect personal information directly from data subjects. Privacy is in scope.

Criterion: P3.1: Personal information is collected consistent with the entity's objectives related to privacy.
Situation B. A SaaS provider has incident response procedures but has never experienced a security incident. The team proposes marking CC7.4 (responds to identified security incidents) as N/A because no incidents occurred during the audit period.

Criterion: CC7.4: Responds to identified security incidents through a defined incident response program.
Situation C. The entity uses cloud-only infrastructure (AWS, with no on-premises facilities). CC6.4 covers physical access to facilities and protected assets. The team proposes marking CC6.4 N/A because the entity has no facilities.

Criterion: CC6.4: Restricts physical access to facilities and protected information assets.
Checkpoint · Highlight

Reviewing proposed N/A reasons

The Northwind Payroll team has drafted reasons for marking criteria N/A. Select the reasons that cannot support an N/A designation. Select a phrase again to clear it.

Draft N/A log, Privacy and Security in scope. P3.1: Northwind receives employee data from its employer customers and never collects it from employees directly; the reason will be stated in the system description. 7.3

The system boundary

In plain terms

A SOC 2 report examines one defined system, so the entity must state exactly what that system includes. The system covers far more than the application: it includes the people, procedures, data, software, and infrastructure that deliver the service. Drawing this boundary is the GRC professional’s way of telling the auditor which parts of the organization will be examined and which will not.

Key terms
System

The infrastructure, software, procedures, and data that are designed, implemented, and operated by people to achieve one or more of the entity’s specific business objectives, such as delivery of services.

System boundaries

The specific aspects of an entity’s infrastructure, software, people, procedures, and data necessary to provide a service. Systems for different services may share components, but each has its own boundary.

System components

The individual elements of a system, grouped into five categories. This course uses the DC Section 200 labels: people, procedures, data, software, and infrastructure.

Definition of a system

In SOC 2 usage, a "system" extends beyond application code. It includes the people who operate it, the procedures that govern it, the data it handles, the software it runs, and the underlying infrastructure. A boundary drawn too narrowly omits controls that auditors expect to see; one drawn too broadly expands the engagement scope unnecessarily.

The five-component model comes from DC Section 200 (the AICPA's Description Criteria for SOC 2 Reports), the companion document to the TSC. The TSC reference each component throughout (CC2.1 explicitly mentions infrastructure, software, data, and organizational roles), and the five-component model provides the structure for defining the boundary of what the engagement examines.

Example

Drawing the boundary for Northwind Payroll

Northwind Payroll runs two products: the payroll platform its customers pay for, and a public marketing website. The GRC lead defines the boundary around the payroll platform only.

  1. In scope: the payroll operations and engineering staff (people); the payroll release and access provisioning procedures (procedures); employee pay records and audit logs (data); the payroll application and its identity provider (software); and the cloud production environment that hosts it (infrastructure).
  2. Out of scope: the marketing website, which shares no customer data with the platform and runs in a separate environment.

The boundary statement records both lists and the reason for the exclusion, so the auditor does not have to infer where the system ends.

People

Personnel involved in operating, maintaining, or using the system.

  • Engineering and operations staff
  • Security and compliance teams
  • Customer success / support roles
  • Outsourced administrators

Procedures

Automated and manual procedures involved in operation.

  • Change management workflow
  • Incident response runbook
  • Access provisioning procedure
  • Backup and recovery procedure

Data

Transaction streams, files, databases, tables, and outputs.

  • Customer data in production database
  • Audit logs and security telemetry
  • Backup and archive storage
  • Generated reports and exports

Software

Application programs, system software, and utilities.

  • Production application code
  • Operating systems and runtimes
  • Build, deploy, and monitoring tools
  • Identity and access management

Infrastructure

Physical and hardware components, including network, servers, and facilities.

  • Cloud compute and storage (AWS, GCP, Azure)
  • Network architecture (VPCs, load balancers)
  • Office facilities (if relevant to scope)
  • Endpoint devices for privileged users
Practice note The boundary diagram is among the most closely scrutinized elements of engagement preparation. It should name the products, environments, third parties, and connection points in scope, and it should state with equal precision what is out of scope and why.

7.4

The system description

In plain terms

The system description is a document, written by the entity’s management, that explains what the system does, what has been promised to customers, what the system contains, and which controls support the criteria. It appears in the SOC 2 report alongside the auditor’s opinion, and the auditor evaluates whether it is accurate. GRC staff usually draft or coordinate it, so they need to know what it must contain.

Key terms
System description

Management’s written narrative of how the system operates and how it meets the categories in scope, prepared in accordance with the description criteria in DC Section 200.

System requirements

Specifications regarding how the system should function to meet the entity’s commitments, comply with relevant laws and regulations, and achieve other relevant objectives. They often follow from service commitments.

Subservice organization

A vendor that performs controls relevant to the service, such as a cloud host responsible for data center security. The description explains how its controls relate to the entity’s own.

Complementary user entity controls (CUECs)

Controls that customers must perform for the entity’s controls to be effective, such as managing the access of the users they add to the platform.

Purpose of the system description

The system description is the written narrative of how the system operates and how it meets the trust services categories in scope. It accompanies the auditor's opinion in a SOC 2 report. The TSC define what controls must accomplish; the description explains what the specific system does and which controls support which criteria.

The structure of the description is governed by DC Section 200, Description Criteria for a Description of a Service Organization's System in a SOC 2® Report, a separate AICPA document. DC Section 200 contains nine description criteria (DC1–DC9). The six most relevant to GRC staff are summarized below.

DC1

Types of services and products provided

Describe the services or products the system delivers, including the purposes for which customers use it, its principal functions, and the channels through which users access it.

DC2

Principal service commitments and system requirements

Document the commitments made to customers (SLAs, performance, and security commitments) and the operational requirements that follow from them. Uptime, response time, and recovery objectives are stated here.

DC3

Components of the system used to provide services

Describe each of the five components (people, procedures, data, software, and infrastructure) for the system in scope, specifying products, environments, and locations.

DC4

System boundaries and key aspects

Define what is in scope and what is excluded. Identify subservice organizations (vendors performing controls relevant to the service) and explain how their controls interact with the entity's own, typically through the "carve-out" or "inclusive" method.

DC5

Identified relevant aspects of internal control

Describe how each Common Criteria component (control environment, communication, risk assessment, monitoring, control activities) operates within the system.

DC6

Complementary user entity controls (CUECs) and subservice controls

Identify controls that customers must perform for the entity's controls to be effective, along with the carve-out subservice organization controls on which the entity relies (e.g., AWS for physical security of data centers).

Example

Outlining the Northwind Payroll description

Northwind Payroll’s GRC lead builds an outline of the description by assigning each fact about the system to the criterion that calls for it.

  1. DC1: Northwind provides payroll calculation and tax withholding for small employers through a web application.
  2. DC2: Northwind commits to 99.5% monthly uptime and to completing each approved payroll run by the customer’s scheduled pay date.
  3. DC3 and DC4: the five components from the boundary exercise, the exclusion of the marketing website, and the cloud host identified as a carved-out subservice organization.
  4. DC6: customers are responsible for submitting accurate hours and for approving each payroll run before release.

The DC6 item needs care. Approving a payroll run is the customer’s decision, so it is a legitimate CUEC. Checking the arithmetic of the calculation is Northwind’s responsibility and could not be listed there.

Note on CUECs Complementary user entity controls acknowledge that certain controls must reside with the customer for the overall system to function, for example, "customers are responsible for establishing strong passwords for their administrative users." Auditors will examine whether any claimed CUEC is in fact a responsibility of the service organization.
Activity · Matching

7.5

Conducting a gap assessment

In plain terms

A gap assessment is a rehearsal conducted before the auditor arrives. The team works through every in-scope criterion, records what the entity does today, and rates each criterion as Met, Partial, or Gap. The result tells leadership how much work remains and becomes the plan for completing it, which makes it one of the most common deliverables a GRC professional produces.

Key terms
Readiness services

Pre-audit work typically performed under the consulting standards. The practitioner develops findings and recommendations for management and does not express an opinion (TSP 100, para. .28).

Gap matrix

The working output of a gap assessment, usually a spreadsheet with one row per criterion recording the current state, the status, and the remediation.

Remediation

The work required to move a Partial or Gap item to Met. Each remediation item carries an owner and a target date.

Readiness assessment

A gap assessment is a structured review of every in-scope criterion to determine whether the entity currently meets it, partially meets it, or has a gap. A well-executed assessment gives leadership a clear picture of effort and timeline; a poorly executed one leaves issues to surface during the audit. TSP 100 refers to this kind of pre-audit work as "readiness services" performed under consulting standards (TSP 100, para. .28).

The output is a gap matrix, typically a spreadsheet with one row per criterion. The assessment uses three statuses:

Met

Met

The criterion is fully addressed. Controls exist, are operating, and produce evidence auditors can sample. No remediation is needed.

Partial

Partial

Some elements are in place, but the criterion is not fully addressed. Examples include a control whose evidence is not captured, a vulnerability process without SLAs, and a runbook that exists but has not been tested. Remediation is targeted and usually brief.

Gap

Gap

The criterion is not addressed. Either no control exists, or the existing control does not achieve the outcome the criterion requires. Remediation typically requires more time and may involve cross-functional work.

Example

Rating one row at Northwind Payroll

The Northwind Payroll team reaches CC9.2 (risks associated with vendors and business partners) in its gap matrix and works through it in order.

  1. Record the current state. The team requests a SOC 2 report from each critical vendor at contract signing, but no one reviews vendors after that, and three contracts have renewed without review.
  2. Compare it with the criterion. An onboarding review exists, so the criterion is partly addressed. Ongoing management of vendor risk is missing.
  3. Assign the status. Some elements are in place and the criterion is not fully addressed, so the row is rated Partial.
  4. Plan the remediation. Define an annual vendor review cadence, review the three renewed vendors first, and name the procurement manager as owner with a 60-day target.

The sample gap matrix below illustrates each status in practice. More rows are marked Partial than Met, which is typical of a first assessment.

Criterion
Current state
Status
Remediation
CC6.2
Quarterly access reviews documented in JIRA; offboarding completed within 24 hours of last day in Workday
Met
Maintain evidence collection
CC7.1
Vulnerability scans run monthly via Tenable; remediation tracked but no defined SLAs by severity
Partial
Define severity-based SLAs (Crit 7d / High 30d / Med 90d) · Owner: Security Eng · Due: 30d
CC7.4
Incident response runbook exists but has not been tested in 18 months
Partial
Conduct tabletop exercise; document results · Owner: Security · Due: 60d
CC8.1

A1.3

CC9.2

Requirements for a credible gap assessment (1) Every in-scope criterion is evaluated, including those the team is confident about, and the supporting evidence is recorded. (2) Partial is a legitimate status; most organizations record more Partial than Met items on a first pass, and items should not be rated higher than the evidence supports. (3) Every Gap or Partial item is assigned an owner and a target date. Without owners and dates, a gap assessment cannot serve as a remediation plan.

Module 8

From Criteria to Controls

The criteria specify the outcomes an entity must achieve; controls are the means by which it achieves them. This module addresses control design, the writing of testable control narratives, and the collection of evidence sufficient for examination.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this module
  • Identify the six elements of a well-written control narrative
  • Classify controls along the manual/automated and preventive/detective axes
  • Map a single control to multiple criteria where appropriate
  • Distinguish vague narratives from testable ones
  • Identify evidence types that demonstrate operating effectiveness
Module 8 · Begin
8.1

The anatomy of a control narrative

In plain terms

The criteria state what must be achieved. A control is what the entity actually does to achieve it, and a control narrative is the written statement of that control. Because auditors test controls against the narrative, it must say clearly who does what, when, how, what record is left behind, and what happens when a problem is found. Writing such narratives is a core GRC task.

Key terms
Criteria

The benchmarks used to measure or evaluate the subject matter. In the TSC, each criterion describes an outcome the entity’s controls should ordinarily meet.

Controls

Policies and procedures that are part of the entity’s system of internal control, whose objective is to provide reasonable assurance that the entity’s objectives are achieved.

Control narrative

The written description of a single control. A testable narrative states six elements: who, what, when, how, evidence, and exception handling.

Principle · Outcomes and controls

TSP 100, para. .03, states: "The trust services criteria set forth the outcomes that an entity's controls should ordinarily meet... regardless of the specific controls implemented by management." The criteria describe outcomes; management selects the controls that achieve them. The glossary defines a control activity as "an action established through policies and procedures that help ensure that management's directives to mitigate risks to the achievement of objectives are carried out."

This flexibility gives organizations latitude, and it places a corresponding burden on the control narrative. Because the criteria do not prescribe specific controls, the narrative must state precisely what the entity does. The most frequent deficiency in control narratives is vagueness: a statement such as "Access is reviewed periodically" conveys almost nothing to an auditor.

A testable control narrative contains six elements. When any element is missing, the control becomes more difficult to test and more open to challenge.

Who
The actor, identified by role
What
The specific action and its scope
When
Frequency or trigger event
How
The method, tool, or system used
Evidence
The artifact created when the control runs
Exception
The handling path when something is found
Example

Rewriting a backup control at Northwind Payroll

Northwind Payroll’s first draft of a backup control reads: “Backups are monitored.” The GRC lead rebuilds it one element at a time.

  1. Who: the Site Reliability Lead.
  2. What: confirms that every scheduled backup of the production payroll database completed.
  3. When: each business day by 10:00.
  4. How: by reviewing the backup job report in the monitoring console.
  5. Evidence: a daily operations ticket recording the review.
  6. Exception: any failed job is logged as an incident ticket and rerun within 24 hours.

The revised narrative is longer, and each added phrase tells the auditor something specific to request or verify.

8.2

Control types: manual/automated × preventive/detective

In plain terms

Controls can be sorted on two simple distinctions. The first is whether a person carries out the control or a system enforces it. The second is whether the control stops a problem before it happens or finds a problem after it has happened. Applying both places every control in one of four groups, and a balanced program uses all four. The TSC themselves note that control activities may combine manual and automated controls, and preventive and detective controls (CC5.1, points of focus).

Key terms
Manual control

A control performed by a person, such as a manager reviewing and approving a request.

Automated control

A control enforced by a system without relying on a person to carry out each instance, such as a login system that requires multi-factor authentication.

Preventive control

A control that stops an unwanted event from occurring.

Detective control

A control that identifies an unwanted event after it has occurred, so that it can be corrected.

Principle · Classification of controls

Each control can be classified along two axes. The first is method: the control is either performed by a person (manual) or enforced by a system (automated). The second is function: the control either prevents an event from occurring (preventive) or identifies an event after it has occurred (detective). Mature programs use all four combinations deliberately. Preventive controls are generally stronger, while detective controls identify events that preventive controls fail to stop.

A pull-request approval that blocks a merge until review is complete is automated and preventive. A weekly review of failed login attempts is manual and detective. CC8.1 (change management) ordinarily relies on both types: pull-request approval prevents unauthorized code from reaching production, and post-deployment monitoring detects issues that were not prevented.

Example

Layering controls over a Northwind payroll run

Northwind Payroll protects each payroll run with three controls that work together.

  1. Automated + Preventive: the platform will not release a payroll run until a customer approver has approved it in the application.
  2. Automated + Detective: after release, a scheduled job compares total pay against the prior run and flags any change larger than a set threshold.
  3. Manual + Detective: a payroll operations analyst reviews each flagged run the same day and contacts the customer when the change is unexplained.

The preventive control blocks unapproved runs. The two detective controls catch an approved run that is still wrong, which the preventive control was never designed to stop.

PREVENTIVE
stops it before it happens
DETECTIVE
identifies it after it happens
MANUAL
performed by a person
AUTOMATED
enforced by a system
Manual + Preventive
Manager approves new vendor before contract signing
Manual + Detective
Quarterly access review by the IT Ops Manager
Automated + Preventive
SSO enforces MFA on every login
Automated + Detective
SIEM alerts on unusual login behavior

8.3

One control, many criteria

In plain terms

Controls and criteria do not pair off one to one. Because each criterion describes an outcome, a single activity can produce several outcomes at once and can therefore support several criteria. GRC staff record these links in a control matrix, which keeps the control set lean and shows the auditor which control addresses which criterion.

Key terms
Control matrix

A table that maps each control to the criteria it addresses. It is the working reference for both the GRC team and the auditor.

Mapping

A documented link between a control and a criterion, with a rationale explaining how the control’s activity produces the outcome the criterion describes.

Common misconception

A frequent misconception in SOC 2 readiness work is that each criterion requires its own control. No such requirement exists. Because the criteria define outcomes, a single well-designed control can produce several outcomes and may therefore map to several criteria. Recognizing this relationship can substantially reduce duplication in a control matrix.

Consider a quarterly access review as a worked example. It is one control, consisting of a single recurring activity, yet that activity addresses several criteria at once. Select each criterion below to view the rationale for the mapping.

Single Control

Quarterly Access Review

The IT Operations Manager reviews the list of users with administrative access to production systems each quarter, comparing IAM rosters against active employee status, escalating discrepancies to data owners.

CC6.2
Registers, authorizes, removes access
Primary mapping. The review identifies users whose roles have changed or who have left, triggering removal of inappropriate access. This access lifecycle is the subject of CC6.2.
CC6.3
Authorizes, modifies, removes access by roles
Secondary mapping. The review verifies that role-based access aligns with current responsibilities, confirming that granted access matches the present requirements of each role.
CC4.1
Selects and performs ongoing or separate evaluations
Monitoring mapping. The quarterly cadence constitutes a periodic separate evaluation of access and therefore addresses CC4.1's requirement for ongoing or separate evaluations of internal control.
CC4.2
Evaluates and communicates control deficiencies
Communication mapping. When the review identifies inappropriate access, escalation to the data owner with documented remediation satisfies the deficiency communication and tracking requirement of CC4.2.
Practice note GRC staff should maintain a control-to-criteria mapping, commonly called a control matrix. Most well-designed controls map to 2–4 criteria. A control that maps to only one criterion may warrant review for sufficiency. A control mapped to eight or more criteria should be examined to confirm that it performs each of those functions in practice.

8.4

Build a testable narrative

In plain terms

A narrative is testable when an outside auditor can read it and know exactly what records to request. Vague wording such as “in a timely manner” or “appropriate personnel” leaves the auditor to guess, and guesses lead to follow-up questions and possible exceptions. This lesson practices replacing vague phrases with specific roles, systems, triggers, timeframes, and records.

Key terms
Service auditor

The independent practitioner who performs the SOC 2 examination and, in a Type 2 engagement, tests the controls and reports the results of those tests.

Trigger event

The occurrence that starts a control that does not run on a fixed schedule, such as an employee’s termination being recorded in the HR system.

Testable narrative

A narrative specific enough that an auditor outside the organization can determine what evidence to request without asking follow-up questions.

Principle · Specificity

Two narratives may describe the same control and yet lead to very different examination outcomes. A vague narrative invites challenge, whereas a specific narrative can be tested. The exercise below uses a CC6.2 offboarding control to illustrate the distinction. Each blank offers three options; as more specific options are selected, the narrative moves from vague to testable.

Example

Testing a vendor review narrative at Northwind Payroll

Northwind Payroll’s draft reads: “Vendors are reviewed regularly.” The GRC lead reads it as an auditor would and lists the questions it leaves open: who performs the review, how often, which vendors, what is reviewed, and where the result is recorded. Each answer becomes part of the revision:

“Each January, the Procurement Manager reviews every vendor on the critical vendor list in the vendor management system, obtaining each vendor’s current SOC 2 report and recording the review and any concerns in the vendor’s record. Concerns are escalated to the Security Lead within 10 business days.”

An auditor can now request the critical vendor list, select vendors from it, and check each vendor’s record for a January review.

Activity · Completion

Select each highlighted blank to cycle through its three options. A blank turns green when the most specific (testable) option is selected. Complete the narrative with all six blanks green.

revokes access for departing employees in , triggered by , with completion documented in , and the IT Operations Manager .

0 of 6 blanks set to the most specific option.
The vague version starts: "Someone removes access for departing employees in a timely manner." The testable version names roles, systems, triggers, timeframes, and evidence.
Criterion for testability A narrative is testable when an auditor outside the organization can read it and determine exactly what evidence to request. If the auditor must ask follow-up questions to establish what the entity does, the narrative requires further revision.
Checkpoint · Highlight

Finding the phrases an auditor would question

Select the phrases that would force an auditor to ask follow-up questions before knowing what evidence to request. Select a phrase again to clear it.

Appropriate personnel review every firewall rule change recorded in the change log in a timely manner, recording each review in a JIRA ticket, and issues are addressed as needed.

8.5

Evidence quality

In plain terms

Evidence is the record that shows a control actually happened. Some records prove this directly, such as system logs with timestamps. Others only show what was supposed to happen, such as a policy. In a Type 2 examination the auditor tests whether controls operated throughout a period of months, so GRC staff must collect strong evidence continuously from the first day of that period.

Key terms
Type 1 report

A SOC 2 report on the description and the suitability of design of controls. It contains no opinion on operating effectiveness and no detailed description of tests of controls.

Type 2 report

A SOC 2 report that adds an opinion on whether controls operated effectively throughout a specified period, with a detailed description of the service auditor’s tests and their results (TSP 100, para. .16).

Operating effectiveness

Whether a control actually functioned as designed, consistently, over the period under examination.

Population and sample

The population is every occurrence of a control during the period. The auditor selects a sample from it and examines the evidence for each selected occurrence.

Context · Type 1 and Type 2 evidence

TSP 100, para. .16, distinguishes the engagement types. A SOC 2 Type 1 examination addresses design at a point in time. A SOC 2 Type 2 examination addresses operating effectiveness over a period (typically 6 or 12 months), and the report includes "a detailed description of tests of controls performed by the service auditor and the results of those tests." Type 2 evidence therefore requires a continuous record across the period. Some evidence directly demonstrates that a control operated; other evidence is supportive and insufficient on its own.

High

Demonstrates operation directly

Difficult to fabricate, date-stamped, and suitable for sampling. The auditor can obtain a population, select a sample, and trace each execution of the control from start to finish.

Medium

Demonstrates operation with caveats

Shows the control was performed but requires supporting context. Strong if it references specific items reviewed; weaker if generic.

Low

Supportive only

Demonstrates what was intended to occur without showing that it did occur. Useful alongside higher-quality evidence; insufficient on its own.

Example

Evidence for Northwind offboarding over a 12-month period

Northwind Payroll is in a 12-month Type 2 period, and its offboarding control requires access to be revoked within 24 hours of an employee’s last day.

  1. The auditor requests the population: every termination recorded in the HR system during the period, 31 in total.
  2. The auditor selects a sample from that list.
  3. For each sampled employee, the team produces the offboarding ticket and the identity provider’s log showing the date and time the account was disabled.

The ticket and the log are high-quality evidence because they are system-generated, dated, and tied to a specific person. The offboarding policy and a screenshot of today’s active user list would show only intent and current state, and neither proves that any sampled revocation happened on time.

Activity · Classification

Assign each evidence type to the appropriate tier

Select an evidence type, then select the quality tier to which it belongs. Select a placed chip to return it to the pool. Deselection and undo work as in the previous activity.

System-generated audit logs with timestamps
JIRA tickets with creator, assignee, and resolution timestamps
Signed and dated quarterly review form citing specific items reviewed
Slack message from manager confirming approval, with thread context
Policy document describing what should happen
Verbal assertion that "we always do this"
Screenshot of the current state of a system
CloudTrail logs of API calls during the audit period
High Quality
Medium Quality
Low Quality
Select an evidence chip, then select the tier to which it belongs.
Practice note · Type 2 evidence (1) Continuous evidence capture: collection should begin at the start of the audit period rather than in its final month. (2) A designated owner for each control: ownership should rest with a named role rather than a team. (3) A central evidence repository: when auditors request samples, staff should be able to retrieve them within minutes.
Checkpoint · Sequence

How Type 2 evidence is tested

Drag the steps into the order in which they occur for one control in a Type 2 examination, or use the arrow buttons.

  1. Each time the control runs during the period, its record is captured in the evidence repository
  2. The auditor requests the population: every occurrence of the control during the period
  3. The auditor selects a sample from the population
  4. The team retrieves the evidence for each sampled occurrence
  5. The auditor examines each item to determine whether the control operated as described

Module 9

Glossary & References

A reference module for ongoing professional use. It contains a searchable glossary, lookup tables of criteria counts, a guide to the authoritative source documents, and a set of flashcards for self-assessment. Because the module is intended for continuing reference, it has no knowledge check.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this module
  • Use precise TSC terminology grounded in the TSP 100 glossary (Appendix A)
  • Determine the criteria count for any series or scope
  • Identify the authoritative source document for a given TSC question
  • Assess recall of core terms using flashcards
Module 9 · Begin
9.1

Glossary

In plain terms

A glossary is a list of terms with their agreed meanings. In SOC 2 work, small differences in wording matter: a control owner, an auditor, and a customer need to mean the same thing when they say "system" or "commitment." This lesson provides a searchable list of the course terms, each marked with its source, so that a practitioner can confirm a definition before using it in a control narrative, a policy, or a conversation with the auditor.

Key terms
TSP 100

The AICPA publication that presents the 2017 Trust Services Criteria with the points of focus revised in 2022. Its Appendix A is the glossary of terms the document defines.

Commitments

Declarations made by management to customers regarding the performance of one or more systems. They may appear in individualized agreements, standardized contracts, service-level agreements, or published statements (TSP 100, Appendix A).

Practitioner

As used in TSP 100, a CPA who performs an examination of controls within an entity's system relevant to security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, or privacy.

Practice term

A term in common SOC 2 use that TSP 100 does not define in Appendix A. Such terms come from related AICPA documents, such as DC Section 200 and the SOC 2 Guide, or from established practice.

Sources of terms

TSP 100 defines 73 terms in Appendix A. Many other terms in common use (CUEC, subservice organization, control narrative, RTO, and RPO, among others) derive from related AICPA documents such as DC Section 200 and the SOC 2 Guide, or from established SOC 2 practice. Each entry below carries a badge identifying its source: PDF denotes a term defined in TSP 100, Appendix A, and Practice denotes complementary industry terminology.

Example

Checking terms while drafting the system description

A GRC analyst at Northwind Payroll is drafting the system description before the company's audit period begins. The draft states that Northwind "commits to 99.9% uptime," and the analyst uses the glossary to confirm that the wording holds up.

  1. She searches "commitments." The entry carries the PDF badge and defines commitments as declarations by management to customers about system performance, including those made in service-level agreements.
  2. She confirms that the uptime figure appears in Northwind's customer SLA, so the sentence describes a genuine commitment.
  3. She then searches "CUEC." The entry carries the Practice badge, which tells her the definition comes from related AICPA guidance, so she notes DC Section 200 as the document to check before finalizing that section.

9.2

Quick lookup tables

In plain terms

These tables answer a frequent planning question: how many criteria will an examination cover? Every SOC 2 scope starts with the 33 Common Criteria, and each additional category adds its own specific criteria on top. Knowing this arithmetic helps a GRC professional size a gap assessment, estimate effort, and correct the common assumption that each category repeats the full set.

Key terms
Common Criteria

The criteria common to all five trust services categories, organized as CC1 through CC9. For the security category they form the complete set, and no additional criteria are needed (TSP 100, para. .10).

Category-specific criteria

The additional criteria for availability (A series), processing integrity (PI series), confidentiality (C series), and privacy (P series). A complete set for one of these categories is the Common Criteria plus its specific criteria (TSP 100, para. .10).

Scope

In practice, the trust services categories and the system that an examination addresses. Scope determines which criteria apply.

Reference · Criteria counts

The criteria counts are stable, and GRC staff benefit from knowing them, since they arise in scoping discussions, readiness assessments, and audit planning. The Common Criteria total 33; category-specific additions span 0 (security) to 18 (privacy). The largest CC series is CC6 (access) at 8 criteria; the smallest is CC8 (change management) at 1 criterion.

Example

Sizing a scope change

Northwind Payroll holds a Security-only SOC 2. An enterprise prospect asks for Availability and Confidentiality in the next report, and the sales lead asks the GRC team how much the scope will grow.

  1. The team starts from the current scope: 33 Common Criteria.
  2. From the category table, Availability adds 3 criteria (A1.1–A1.3) and Confidentiality adds 2 (C1.1–C1.2).
  3. The new total is 33 + 3 + 2 = 38, which matches the scope table row for Security + Availability + Confidentiality.
  4. The gap assessment therefore gains five new rows. The 33 Common Criteria already in the matrix are not repeated.

9.3

Source documents to bookmark

In plain terms

This course summarizes several AICPA and COSO documents, and those documents remain the authority when a question arises at work. Each answers a different kind of question. The TSC define the criteria; DC Section 200 governs the system description; COSO explains the internal control principles behind CC1–CC5; and the AT-C standards and AICPA guides govern how the examination is performed. Knowing which document to open saves time and keeps interpretations defensible.

Key terms
Description criteria

The criteria in DC Section 200 (DC1–DC9) that specify what a SOC 2 system description must address. A SOC 2 examination reports on whether the description is in accordance with them (as described in the definition of a SOC 2 examination, TSP 100, Appendix A).

Attestation standards

The AICPA professional standards, issued as AT-C sections, under which practitioners perform examination engagements. A SOC 2 examination is performed in accordance with them (as described in the definition of a SOC 2 examination, TSP 100, Appendix A).

COSO

The Committee of Sponsoring Organizations of the Treadway Commission. Its 2013 Internal Control: Integrated Framework contains the 17 principles to which the trust services criteria are aligned (TSP 100, para. .08).

Authoritative sources

This course introduces the material; the source documents remain the authority. Questions that arise in practice, such as whether a criterion applies or what qualifies as a CUEC, should be resolved by reference to the documents below, which practitioners cite as canonical. Select each card to view its scope and the circumstances in which to consult it.

Example

Routing three audit-preparation questions

In the month before fieldwork, the Northwind Payroll GRC lead receives three questions and sends each to the document that governs it.

  1. A control owner asks for the exact points of focus under CC6.1. The answer is in the TSC document itself.
  2. The writer of the system description asks what the description must say about subservice organizations. That question falls under DC Section 200.
  3. The CFO asks how the auditor is likely to approach sampling. The AICPA SOC 2 Reporting Guide addresses sampling and testing approaches.
Primary

2017 TSC with Revised Points of Focus (2022)

AICPA · ASEC
The TSC document itself and the currently applicable standard for SOC 2, SOC 3, SOC for Cybersecurity, and SOC for Supply Chain. It defines all 33 Common Criteria, the 28 category-specific criteria across A, PI, C, and P, the points of focus, and the application guidance. Consult it for: the exact text of a criterion, the official list of points of focus, or paragraph-level guidance on applying a criterion.
Companion

DC Section 200: Description Criteria for SOC 2

AICPA
The companion to the TSC. It defines the nine description criteria (DC1–DC9), which specify what a SOC 2 system description must address: types of services, service commitments, system components, boundaries, aspects of internal control, CUECs, and subservice organizations. Consult it for: drafting or reviewing the system description, defining boundaries, or determining what to include in CUECs.
Foundation

COSO Internal Control: Integrated Framework (2013)

Committee of Sponsoring Organizations
The source of the 17 principles, across 5 components, to which CC1–CC5 align one-to-one. TSP 100 references COSO throughout; where a criterion reads "COSO Principle N," it refers to this document. Consult it for: fuller explanation of any CC1–CC5 principle, or for explaining to leadership how the foundation of SOC 2 relates to broader internal control theory.
Standards

AT-C 105 / 205 / 320

AICPA Professional Standards
The attestation standards governing how SOC engagements are performed. AT-C 105 covers concepts common to all attestation engagements (suitable criteria, practitioner responsibilities). AT-C 205 covers assertion-based examination engagements. AT-C 320 covers SOC 1 and other engagement requirements specific to service organizations. Consult it for: questions about a practitioner's professional responsibilities, or engagement planning with a service auditor.
Practitioner Guide

AICPA SOC 2® Reporting Guide

AICPA · Updated periodically
The AICPA's authoritative practitioner guide for planning, performing, and reporting on SOC 2 engagements. It covers engagement acceptance, materiality, sampling, testing approaches, and report formats. Consult it for: audit preparation, particularly anticipating auditor expectations regarding testing approach, evidence requests, and reporting.
Specialty

SOC for Cybersecurity Guide

AICPA
The AICPA guide for SOC for Cybersecurity examinations. These examinations differ from SOC 2 in that they address an entity-wide cybersecurity risk management program rather than a specific service organization system. Consult it for: engagements at the entity level rather than the system level, or scoping decisions that weigh a cybersecurity risk management program against a service organization system.

10.2

Five mental models for TSC practice

In plain terms

A mental model is a short rule that helps a practitioner reason quickly through a new situation. This lesson condenses the course into five such rules, covering how criteria are counted, how criteria relate to controls, how narratives become testable, how controls map to criteria, and what makes evidence strong. GRC staff use them to test proposals and answer stakeholder questions without reopening every module.

Key terms
Mental model

A compact, reusable principle that guides reasoning across many situations. The five in this lesson are drawn from the preceding modules.

Control matrix

In practice, a table that lists each control and the criteria it supports. It is used to find duplication and gaps in coverage.

Principles

Five reusable mental models emerge from the preceding modules. They apply in scoping discussions, planning meetings, reviews of vendor SOC reports, and disagreements with auditors. Select each card to see how the model applies.

Example

Evaluating a proposed change to code review

The engineering lead at Northwind Payroll proposes replacing a manual approval spreadsheet with branch protection that blocks any merge to production without a second reviewer. The GRC lead evaluates the proposal against the models.

  1. Model 2: the question is whether the new control meets the outcome CC8.1 describes for authorizing and approving changes. A different mechanism from the old one raises no problem in itself.
  2. Model 3: the narrative is rewritten to name who reviews, what is approved, when, how, what evidence is produced, and how exceptions are handled.
  3. Model 5: system-generated merge records replace the spreadsheet, so the evidence now comes directly from the system.
  4. Model 4: the control matrix is updated to record CC8.1 and any other criteria the control genuinely supports, without crediting it with more.
01

The Common Criteria are shared across all categories.

Adding a category adds its category-specific criteria and never duplicates the 33 Common Criteria.

Typical use: Scoping discussions, audit preparation budgets, and explanations of cost to leadership. A stakeholder may assume that adding Privacy doubles the work. The 33 Common Criteria are already in scope for Security, and Privacy adds 18 specific criteria to that existing set.
02

Criteria describe outcomes; controls are the means of achieving them.

TSP 100, para. .03 states that the TSC do not prescribe specific controls. Each entity selects controls on the basis of its own risks.

Typical use: When a vendor promotes a "SOC 2 in a box" template, when an auditor asks why a control differs from another company's, or when a developer asks whether an approach is acceptable. The governing test is whether the control meets the outcome the criterion describes. If it does, the specific implementation is acceptable.
03

Specificity makes a control testable.

Each vague verb ("monitors," "ensures") is a likely future audit finding. The six-element framework (Who/What/When/How/Evidence/Exception) makes narratives testable.

Typical use: Review of every control narrative the team writes. The test is whether an outside reader could identify what evidence to request. If not, the narrative requires further work. Applied early, this discipline can save weeks of audit cycles.
04

A single control typically maps to several criteria.

Most well-designed controls map to 2–4 criteria. Recognizing this reduces duplication and reveals gaps sooner.

Typical use: Building or reviewing a control matrix. A matrix with dozens of one-criterion, one-control rows indicates unnecessary effort. A control mapped to 8 or more criteria is probably credited with more than it does. Well-designed controls generally fall within the range of 2–4 criteria.
05

Evidence quality outweighs evidence volume.

A small set of system-generated logs and ticketed workflows provides stronger evidence than hundreds of policy documents and screenshots.

Typical use: Establishing evidence collection at the start of the audit period. The common tendency is to over-collect. Sound practice is to collect fewer, higher-quality artifacts that demonstrate operation directly, planned backward from the question of what an auditor would sample.
Checkpoint · Highlight

Testing a planning memo against the models

A planning memo for next year's program contains the statements below. Select the statements that conflict with one of the five mental models. Select a phrase again to clear it.

Next year we will add Availability. Because each category repeats the Common Criteria, adding Availability will roughly double the number of criteria to test. Our access review will use a different tool from the one our peer company uses, provided it meets the outcome the criterion describes. To save effort, the quarterly access review will be mapped to eleven criteria. Each narrative will name the reviewer, the action, the frequency, the method, the evidence, and how exceptions are handled. For evidence, we will gather as many policy documents and screenshots as possible.

10.3

Applying the criteria at work: role-based playbooks

In plain terms

A playbook is an ordered list of actions for a situation that recurs. This lesson offers five: preparing a first SOC 2, running an annual program, reviewing a vendor's report, explaining SOC 2 to non-GRC colleagues, and settling into a new GRC role. Each one turns the course material into concrete first steps, so that a GRC professional facing one of these situations knows where to begin.

Key terms
Playbook

A sequenced set of actions for a recurring situation. The playbooks here list the highest-value actions and do not attempt to be comprehensive.

Readiness review

A review before the examination in which a practitioner helps management prepare. Such engagements are typically performed under the consulting standards, and the practitioner provides findings and recommendations without expressing an opinion (TSP 100, para. .28).

Bridge letter

In practice, a letter from a service organization's management that covers the interval between the end of its most recent report period and a later date, used when the report is no longer current.

Context

The five playbooks below address common organizational situations and identify concrete next steps for each. Each playbook lists the highest-value actions for the first 30, 60, and 90 days and does not attempt to be comprehensive. Select a tab to view a playbook.

Example

Applying the vendor playbook

Northwind Payroll receives the SOC 2 report of a vendor that hosts its document storage, and the GRC analyst works through the "five items to check first."

  1. The audit period ended three months ago, so the report is current.
  2. Only Security is in scope. Northwind relies on the vendor's uptime commitment, so the missing Availability category is recorded as a gap to raise with the vendor.
  3. The report is a Type 2 with an unqualified opinion. The analyst still reads the test results and finds an exception in the vendor's access review testing, which she notes for follow-up.
  4. The CUEC section states that customers must review their own user accounts in the vendor's application. Northwind adds that review to its own control set.
90-Day Playbook

Preparing for a first SOC 2 examination

Audience: GRC professionals at organizations preparing a first SOC 2 without an existing program. The usual drivers are enterprise prospects, regulatory commitments, or a board mandate.

Days 1–30 · Scope and Plan
  • Decide categories. Use the Module 7 decision tree. Document the categories in scope and the rationale for each, signed by an executive sponsor.
  • Define the system boundary. Draft the DC4 boundary statement, covering products in scope, environments, subservice organizations, and explicit exclusions.
  • Charter the program. Name an executive sponsor, a program lead, and control owners across departments. Assign every control to a named role.
  • Select a target audit period. Choose Type 1 first if a deliverable is needed within 4–6 months; choose Type 2 if the organization can wait 6–12 months and requires operating-effectiveness evidence.
  • Begin the gap assessment. Use the Module 7 three-status matrix (Met / Partial / Gap), with one row per criterion in scope.
Days 31–60 · Gap and Remediate
  • Complete the gap assessment. Evaluate every in-scope criterion, including those that appear well controlled, and record the supporting evidence.
  • Sequence remediation. Address gaps first, then partial items. Assign each item an owner and a target date, and prioritize by the audit period start date.
  • Rewrite control narratives. Apply the six-element test to every control. A narrative that cannot be tested cannot be audited.
  • Set up evidence collection. For each control, determine where the evidence resides, who captures it, and how it is sampled. Configure log retention, ticket templates, and naming conventions.
  • Select a service auditor. Request proposals from 2–3 firms. Relevant selection criteria include industry experience, partner involvement, fee structure, and references from prior engagements.
Days 61–90 · Execute and Document
  • Draft the system description. Follow the DC1–DC9 structure. The auditor will review the draft and request changes; early drafting allows time for revision.
  • Complete remediation of gaps before audit period start. Partials may be acceptable if remediated during the period; gaps need to be in place before the period begins.
  • Run a readiness review. Conduct the review internally or with the audit firm; a review by the audit firm is often performed under consulting standards (TSP 100, para. .28).
  • Communicate to leadership. Provide a quarterly update covering confirmed scope, closed gaps, the scheduled audit kickoff, and the expected report date.
  • Set the audit period. The audit period begins. From this point, evidence is captured continuously and control owners meet monthly for check-ins.
Quarterly Rhythm

Running an existing SOC 2 program annually

Audience: GRC teams maintaining a recurring SOC 2 Type 2. The principal challenge is sustaining control discipline between audit cycles.

Q1 · Plan and Refresh
  • Refresh the risk assessment. CC3.2 explicitly requires this. Identify changes in products, vendors, regulations, and threats since the last assessment.
  • Review scope. Confirm that the categories remain appropriate, identify systems to add or retire, and document any change with its rationale.
  • Reaffirm control owners. Personnel change roles over time. Confirm that every control has a named, current owner.
  • Plan evidence collection. Identify the evidence required, when it is needed, where it resides, and who captures it.
Q2 · Mid-Year Self-Assessment
  • Sample evidence internally. Select 3–5 controls per series and pull evidence for the past quarter. The evidence for each control should be retrievable in under an hour.
  • Run a tabletop exercise. A1.3 is the most common availability finding because DR plans often go untested. Schedule a live or paper-based tabletop exercise and document the results.
  • Vendor reassessment. CC9.2 requires periodic vendor risk review. Collect annual SOC reports, review exceptions, and reaffirm inherited CUECs.
  • Quarterly access review. Perform the CC6.2 review every quarter, independent of the audit schedule. Document discrepancies and remediation timeframes.
Q3 · Pre-Audit Dry Run
  • Update the system description. Reflect changes since the prior year, including new systems, commitments, and subservice organizations.
  • Internal walkthrough. Walk through every in-scope control with its owner, review an evidence sample, and record any gaps.
  • Pre-audit kickoff. Confirm the timeline, principal deliverables, and expected sample sizes with the audit firm.
Q4 · Audit and Close-Out
  • Audit fieldwork. Respond to requests promptly and designate a single point of contact for evidence requests.
  • Address findings immediately. Assign remediation plans and target dates to all findings, including non-material ones.
  • Lessons-learned debrief. Record the difficulties of the current cycle and the changes planned for the next, and document both for the next program lead.
  • Distribute the report. Provide the report to customers, inform sales of its availability, and have legal review any restrictions on distribution.
Vendor Risk

Reviewing a vendor's SOC 2 report

Audience: anyone who receives a vendor's SOC 2 report and must determine what it establishes. The report is dense, and the most relevant information appears on a small number of pages.

Five items to check first

  • Audit period. Confirm that the period is current. A report covering a period that ended 18 months ago is stale; request a bridge letter or wait for the next report.
  • Scope. Confirm that the report covers the categories your organization requires (Security, Availability, and so on). Some vendors have only Security in scope; if the organization depends on availability commitments, this is a gap.
  • System scope. Confirm that the report covers the specific product or system in use. Vendors sometimes examine only their flagship product, and legacy or specialty products may be excluded.
  • Type 1 or Type 2. A Type 1 report addresses design only; a Type 2 report addresses operating effectiveness over a period. A Type 2 report is usually preferable from a vendor.
  • Auditor opinion. Determine whether the opinion is unqualified ("clean") or qualified. A qualification often appears in a single sentence on a single page and is easily overlooked.

Three items to read closely

  • Exceptions in the test results. Type 2 reports include detailed test results. Any exception ("the auditor noted X in N samples") warrants attention, even when the opinion is clean.
  • Inherited CUECs. The report includes a section identifying Complementary User Entity Controls. These are controls the user entity must operate for the vendor's controls to function. List them and confirm that corresponding controls are in place.
  • Subservice organizations. If the vendor relies on subservice organizations (carve-out method), their coverage may affect the user entity's own SOC scope and risk profile.

Three warning signs that warrant follow-up

  • Significant exceptions in CC6 (access). Failures in identity controls usually indicate deeper weaknesses in the security program.
  • Recurring exceptions year over year. A finding that appears in two consecutive years indicates that the vendor is not remediating effectively.
  • An extensive list of CUECs resembling core security controls. When a vendor assigns many foundational controls to its customers, request an explanation.
Stakeholder Communication

Translating TSC to non-GRC stakeholders

Audience: GRC staff explaining SOC 2 work to engineering, sales, leadership, or the board. Each audience has different concerns, and the message should address those concerns directly.

Engineering

What they want to know: Will this slow me down?

"SOC 2 largely formalizes practices the team would adopt in any case: pull request approvals, change tickets, access reviews, and vulnerability remediation SLAs. Most of the required evidence is observable in systems already in use, such as GitHub, JIRA, Datadog, and Okta. The effort lies in documenting these practices clearly and maintaining them during busy periods. The greatest burden arises when evidence is not captured at the time and must be reconstructed later, so evidence should be captured as the work proceeds."

Sales / Customer Success

What they want to know: What can I promise customers? What if they ask for something we do not have?

"It is accurate to state that we hold a SOC 2 [Type 1/Type 2] report covering [Security + Availability + ...] and that the report can be shared under NDA. If a prospect asks about a category outside our scope (for example, Privacy), state plainly that it is not in scope; if it is a deciding factor in the deal, we can consider adding it in the next cycle. Avoid making promises based on the report's commitments section unless those commitments have been read carefully."

Leadership / CFO

What they want to know: What does this cost? What does it get us?

"An annual SOC 2 Type 2 costs roughly $75K–$200K in audit fees, depending on scope, plus internal staff time. The benefits are that enterprise prospects require it (a direct revenue effect), it reduces vendor security questionnaires (saving sales time), and it provides external assurance to the board. On the cost side, it requires ongoing operational discipline, and the first-year program costs more in remediation than the steady state. The criteria are outcome-based, and the choice of how to meet them rests with us, which allows the program to reflect our risk appetite."

Board / Audit Committee

What they want to know: Are we adequately controlled? Where's the risk?

"SOC 2 examines whether our controls meet the AICPA's trust services criteria, a set of outcomes covering security, availability, and other categories. The criteria align with the COSO framework (CC1–CC5). Our most recent report opinion is [unqualified/qualified]. Of [N] criteria in scope, we had [N] exceptions, all remediated within [timeframe]. Top three areas of ongoing investment: [areas]. Next year's program adds [scope changes] driven by [business reasons]."

First 30 Days

Priorities for a new member of a GRC team

Audience: GRC professionals new to an organization with an existing or upcoming SOC 2. The first month is devoted to listening and learning; substantive contributions begin in the second.

Week 1 · Read
  • The most recent SOC 2 report. Read it in full, noting the scope, opinion, exceptions, CUECs, and subservice organizations.
  • The prior year's gap assessment. Identify the gaps found, the items remediated, and the items still open.
  • The system description. Compare it with how the system operates; the two often diverge in places.
  • The risk assessment. Determine whether it is current, who owns it, and when it was last refreshed.
Week 2 · Meet
  • The executive sponsor. Clarify the sponsor's expectations at 30, 60, and 90 days.
  • Each identifiable control owner. Walk through one control with each owner: the activity performed, the evidence captured, and where that evidence resides.
  • The audit firm partner. Discuss upcoming activities, any concerns from the prior year, and the start date of the next audit period.
  • Engineering leadership. Identify their principal difficulties with the GRC function and the points at which control discipline tends to lapse.
Week 3 · Test
  • Pull evidence samples. Select 5 controls at random and request evidence for the past quarter from their owners. Note how long retrieval takes and how complete the evidence is.
  • Walk a control end to end. Select the highest-risk control and trace the workflow from trigger to evidence to monitoring.
  • Test access reviews. Obtain the prior quarter's access review and determine whether it was complete, whether exceptions were tracked, and whether discrepancies were resolved.
Week 4 · Plan
  • Document the top 3 risks. Base them on the observations from the first three weeks and frame them in TSC criterion language.
  • Propose 3 priority improvements. Candidates include quick fixes, tighter narratives, and evidence improvements with high impact and low cost.
  • Brief the sponsor. Deliver a 30-day report covering findings, proposals, and the support required.
  • Set the cadence. Establish monthly control owner check-ins and quarterly self-assessments to sustain the program between audits.

10.5

Where to go from here

In plain terms

The criteria themselves change rarely, while the practice around them changes often. This lesson lists six habits that keep a GRC professional current after the course: returning to the source documents, following practitioner communities, practicing the core techniques, studying related frameworks, training colleagues, and exercising judgment. Together they turn a single course into continuing professional development.

Key terms
Process or control framework

A set of processes or controls, established by another party such as an industry group, regulator, or standard-setting body, that organizations are expected to implement (TSP 100, Appendix A). The TSC differ in that they set out outcomes and leave the choice of controls to the entity (TSP 100, para. .03).

Control mapping

In practice, a record of which controls satisfy requirements in more than one framework. It allows one control to support several audits.

Continuing development

The TSC change infrequently, while the practice around them evolves continually through new AICPA guidance, audit firm interpretations, control technology, and regulatory pressure. Remaining current is part of professional GRC work.

Example

An annual development plan

After its first SOC 2 cycle, the Northwind Payroll GRC lead writes a one-page development plan for the coming year. It schedules a full reading of CC6 and CC8, the series behind most of the team's evidence requests. Because a European prospect has asked about ISO 27001, the plan adds a mapping of existing controls to that framework, starting with access and change management. It also commits the team to a 30-minute SOC 2 explainer for new engineering hires each quarter.

Read the source documents

Keep the TSC PDF, DC Section 200, the AT-C standards, and the AICPA SOC 2 Reporting Guide readily available. Read the most frequently used criteria in full at least once a year so that interpretation remains grounded in the source.

Follow practitioner communities

Relevant sources include the AICPA SOC community, audit firm publications, and communities associated with security certification tracks. Identify 3–5 practitioners whose interpretations are well regarded and follow their publications.

Practice the discipline

Apply the six-element test to every control narrative written or reviewed. In every control matrix, count the criterion mappings per control. In every gap assessment, apply the Met / Partial / Gap classification consistently. Proficiency develops through repeated application.

Study adjacent frameworks

SOC 2 is closely related to ISO 27001, NIST CSF, FedRAMP, and HITRUST. Most controls map across these frameworks, and an understanding of the mapping improves effectiveness and reduces audit fatigue. Begin with the framework most relevant to the organization's customer base.

Build internal training

GRC work is more effective when engineering, sales, and leadership share a basic understanding of SOC 2. A 30-minute internal explainer on what a SOC 2 is and why it matters, delivered annually and to new hires, repays its cost.

Exercise professional judgment

TSP 100, para. .03 concludes: "applying the trust services criteria in actual situations requires judgment." No flowchart substitutes for that judgment. The framework informs decisions without making them. GRC staff should reason carefully, document that reasoning, and stand by the resulting decisions.

Applying the course in practice

The course has covered ten modules, 33 Common Criteria, 28 category-specific criteria, and 93 glossary terms, along with the distinctions between vague and testable control narratives, between Type 1 and Type 2 reports, and between criteria and points of focus. The remaining work is a matter of judgment: applying these tools to specific systems, risks, and stakeholders. Module 9 remains available for ongoing reference.
